domains.name: Publication & Dissemination
domains.summary: Publication & Dissemination covers the genres, practices and politics through which research reaches readers and is examined and funded: the publishing process, journal choice, the occluded genres around submission (cover letters, reviewer reports, responses to reviewers), open-research statements, conference abstracts and conference participation, the doctoral viva and thesis corrections, turning theses into articles, authorship and contributorship, funding applications, public engagement and academic self-presentation, including personal statements for postgraduate study. Many of these genres are hidden from novices because they are rarely published, so making exemplars and expectations visible is central to teaching. The domain also addresses the opportunities and inequities multilingual scholars meet in English-medium publishing (Flowerdew 1999; Lillis & Curry 2010) and treats them as structural issues, not individual deficits.
domains.learnerSummary: You will learn how research gets published, examined and funded, and how to write and speak in the texts and events involved, from cover letters to conference questions.

stageEmphasis.in-sessional-ug: Focus on personal statements and short academic CVs for postgraduate applications, with a brief introduction to how research is published for students considering research careers.
stageEmphasis.in-sessional-pgt: Introduce the publishing process, authorship, conference abstracts and open-research requirements, and support doctoral and scholarship applications for students planning research careers.
stageEmphasis.pgr: Make this the core: publishing and peer review in both roles, conference participation, turning thesis chapters into articles, the viva and corrections, funding applications, engagement, and the politics of publishing in English.

domains.name: Research Writing
domains.summary: Research Writing covers the part-genres, macrostructures and practices through which postgraduate and early-career writers report and position their own research: introductions built on CARS-type moves, literature reviews, framework and methods sections, results, discussions, conclusions, abstracts, theses (including theses by publication), proposals, systematic and scoping reviews, and research instruments. Move analyses (Swales 1990, 2004; Kanoksilapatham 2005; Yang & Allison 2003; Kwan 2006) are descriptive models to test against disciplinary exemplars, not templates, and IMRaD is dominant in experimental fields but far from universal. The domain also covers the sociopragmatic and self-regulatory work of doctoral candidature, such as supervision, progression reviews, teaching as a graduate teaching assistant, sustaining output and writing reflexively, which Kamler and Thomson (2014) treat as both text work and identity work.
domains.learnerSummary: You will learn how dissertations, theses and research articles are organised in your field and how to write each part. You will also prepare for doctoral progress reviews and for teaching.

stageEmphasis.pre-sessional-ug: Not normally taught as research writing: undergraduate-entry courses build the report, summary and essay skills it later draws on, and any project abstract can use the core abstract moves.
stageEmphasis.pre-sessional-pg: Focus on how research articles are organised (IMRaD and its variants), short introductions that establish a gap, research questions and instrument wording for small projects and, for prospective doctoral students, the research proposal.
stageEmphasis.in-sessional-ug: Support final-year projects and dissertations with methods, results, discussion and abstract writing, anchored in departmental exemplars and the module's own reporting conventions.
stageEmphasis.in-sessional-pgt: Treat the master's dissertation as the main site: research questions and the gap, the literature review as argument, methods and results, calibrated discussion and the abstract, with structured reviews, instruments and ethics documents where the design requires them.
stageEmphasis.pgr: Move to thesis macrostructure and theses by publication, framework chapters, introductions and claims of contribution, progression reviews, supervision, teaching as a graduate teaching assistant and the sustained drafting of a long document.

topics.name: The academic publishing process
topics.description: Understand the stages through which a manuscript becomes a publication — submission, editorial screening and desk rejection, peer review (single-anonymous, double-anonymous, open or transparent, and models such as registered reports and review of preprints), decisions (accept, minor or major revision, reject and resubmit, reject), revision, acceptance, production and post-publication correction or retraction — and the roles of editors, reviewers and authors in each. Understanding the process as a negotiation within a discourse community helps novice authors interpret decisions, plan timelines and avoid treating rejection as a final verdict on their work.
masteryEvidence: Describes the stages of the publication process in their target field, including typical timescales and decision types
Distinguishes the roles and responsibilities of editors, reviewers and authors at each stage
Interprets a decision letter correctly, including what a 'major revision' or 'reject and resubmit' invites the author to do
Identifies field-specific differences, for example conference proceedings in computer science, monographs in the humanities and preprint servers in physics
Explains post-publication processes such as corrections, retractions and open peer review in relation to research integrity
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give the learner an anonymised decision letter (major revision) with three reviewer reports. Ask what the editor is asking for, which comments are essential to address and what the realistic next steps and timescale are. Check whether they read the decision as an invitation to revise and distinguish the editor's priorities from individual reviewers' preferences.

topics.name: Selecting a journal
topics.description: Choose a target journal by matching the manuscript's contribution, method and audience to a journal's aims and scope, readership, article types, recent content, review practices, indexing, open-access options and costs, and turnaround, while screening out predatory or deceptive venues. Writers then read and apply the author guidelines and shape the manuscript for that journal's conversation, ideally choosing the journal before drafting rather than after.
masteryEvidence: Produces a shortlist of three journals with a justified ranking based on scope, audience, article type and recent content
Analyses recent issues of a target journal to identify the conversations the manuscript would join
Recognises warning signs of predatory or deceptive journals and verifies indexing and membership claims
Extracts the requirements in author guidelines (length, structure, referencing, data availability, declarations) and applies them to a manuscript
Weighs open-access routes and article processing charges against funder requirements and available support
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give the learner a manuscript abstract and three candidate journals, one of them with predatory characteristics. Ask them to rank the journals and justify the ranking in five minutes. Check whether they use scope and recent content rather than prestige alone and whether they detect and explain the problematic venue.

topics.name: Cover letters to editors
topics.description: Write submission letters that identify the manuscript and article type, state concisely what it contributes and why it fits the journal's scope and readership, and make the declarations the journal requires (originality, no simultaneous submission, conflicts of interest, ethics, data availability, suggested or excluded reviewers). The letter is an occluded genre, rarely seen by novices, whose readers are busy editors deciding whether to send a paper for review, so it must be brief, specific and professional.
masteryEvidence: Writes a cover letter of one page or less that names the manuscript, article type and journal
States the contribution and its relevance to the journal's readers in two or three specific sentences, referring to the journal's scope or recent content
Includes all declarations required by the journal's instructions, accurately
Uses a formal, confident register without excessive deference or overclaiming
Avoids pasting the abstract as the body of the letter
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give the learner a weak cover letter that pastes the abstract, is effusively deferential and omits a required declaration. Ask them to revise it for a named journal. Check whether the revision states fit and contribution specifically, includes the declaration and adopts a professional register.

topics.name: Responding to reviewers
topics.description: Write response-to-reviewer letters that thank reviewers, address every comment point by point, describe precisely what was changed and where, and explain politely and with evidence when a requested change has not been made. The genre requires managing face, since authors must disagree with gatekeepers while remaining cooperative, as well as clear organisation and consistency between the response and the revised manuscript.
masteryEvidence: Organises a response with each reviewer comment reproduced or summarised, followed by a response and the location of the change
Describes revisions specifically, quoting new text or giving page and line numbers
Declines or partly accepts a requested change with a reasoned, evidence-based and polite explanation
Uses appreciation and mitigation strategically without effusive or formulaic deference
Reconciles conflicting reviewer requests and explains the resolution to the editor
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give the learner two reviewer comments, one reasonable and one that misreads the study, and ask for a response to each. Check whether the first is accepted with a precise description of the change, and whether the second is declined or clarified politely, with evidence, without defensiveness and without capitulating to an unjustified request.

topics.name: Writing peer review reports
topics.description: Write reviewer reports for journals or conferences that summarise the manuscript and its claimed contribution, evaluate its significance, methods, evidence and argument, distinguish major from minor issues, make actionable suggestions and give a recommendation consistent with the comments. Reports must be constructive, appropriately mitigated and respectful, and reviewers must meet ethical obligations of confidentiality, competence, timeliness and disclosure of conflicts of interest.
masteryEvidence: Opens with a fair summary of the manuscript's aims, methods, findings and claimed contribution
Separates major concerns that affect the validity of conclusions from minor and presentational points
Phrases criticism as specific, actionable suggestions with reasons, using mitigation without obscuring the point
Gives a recommendation consistent with the severity of the comments

Identifies the ethical obligations of reviewers, including confidentiality (for example not sharing the manuscript or uploading it to generative AI tools unless the journal explicitly permits this), declaring competing interests and involving co-reviewers only with the editor's permission
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give the learner a short manuscript extract with one serious methodological flaw and several minor issues, and ask for a 300-word review. Check whether the flaw is identified as major and explained, whether minor points are separated, whether the tone is constructive and whether the recommendation matches the comments.

topics.name: Conference abstracts
topics.description: Write abstracts and proposals for conference submission that persuade reviewers of relevance to the conference theme, interest and feasibility, often before the research is complete. Writers adapt the research-abstract moves to a call for papers: framing the topic for the conference audience, stating the aim and approach, reporting results or expected outcomes honestly, and signalling what attendees will gain, within strict word limits and format requirements.
masteryEvidence: Analyses a call for papers and identifies the theme, strands, criteria and format requirements
Writes an abstract within the word limit that links the work to the conference theme and audience
Reports preliminary or expected findings with appropriate tense and hedging, without promising results not yet obtained
Signals the presentation's value to attendees, such as a finding, method, implication or discussion point
Adjusts the abstract for different submission types, such as paper, poster, panel or work in progress
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give the learner a call for papers and their research summary (data collection still in progress) and ask for a 250-word abstract. Check whether it connects to the theme, states the aim and approach, handles incomplete results honestly with future or hedged language and signals what the audience will gain.

topics.name: Thesis defence and viva
topics.description: Prepare for and take part in the oral examination of a thesis: understanding the local format and possible outcomes, re-reading the thesis strategically, anticipating questions about contribution, design, findings, limitations and future work, and answering by explaining, defending, conceding and clarifying in extended spoken interaction with expert examiners. Formats vary widely, from closed UK-style vivas with internal and external examiners, whose recommendation follows the oral, to public defences in much of continental Europe that take place only after a committee has approved the written thesis, often with one or more opponents, and committee defences in North America that follow earlier proposal defences or qualifying examinations, while in some systems, such as many Australian universities, there is no oral examination.
masteryEvidence: Describes the format (including online or hybrid arrangements), participants, procedures and possible outcomes of the viva or defence in their institution, and what happens afterwards, such as how required corrections are specified, made and approved
Summarises the thesis, its contribution and its limitations orally in two to three minutes
Answers challenging questions by clarifying the question, giving a direct answer and supporting it with reference to the thesis
Concedes valid criticisms without abandoning the thesis's main claims and defends choices with reasons
Manages extended interaction, including asking for clarification, taking time to think and navigating to relevant pages
topics.assessmentPrompt: Run a 15–20-minute mock viva with three questions: one open (summarise your contribution), one challenging (why not method X?) and one about a genuine limitation. Follow each answer with at least one probing follow-up, including one that requires the candidate to find and use a specific passage in the thesis. Check whether the learner answers directly, supports answers with reference to the thesis, concedes appropriately and maintains the main claims.

topics.name: Authorship and contribution
topics.description: Understand what qualifies someone for authorship, using criteria such as the ICMJE's, and how contributions are described with contributor-role taxonomies such as CRediT (which record who did what but do not by themselves decide who qualifies as an author), how author order conventions differ across disciplines, and what counts as honorary, guest or ghost authorship. Researchers should be able to discuss authorship early in collaborations, including with supervisors, and to write accurate contribution statements and acknowledgements, including declarations of the use of AI tools, which journals do not accept as authors.
masteryEvidence: Applies a published authorship standard to decide whether a set of described contributions qualifies for authorship or acknowledgement
Writes a contributor statement using CRediT roles for a multi-author paper
Explains author-order conventions in their field and how they differ elsewhere, for example alphabetical order, first and last positions or equal contribution
Identifies honorary, guest and ghost authorship as integrity problems
Opens an authorship conversation with collaborators or supervisors early in a project, using appropriate pragmatic strategies
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give the learner a scenario describing five people's contributions to a paper (data collection only, supervision only, analysis and drafting, funding acquisition, critical revision) and ask who should be an author and who should be acknowledged, according to ICMJE. Check whether they apply all the criteria rather than only effort, and whether they note field variation.

topics.name: Publishing as a multilingual scholar
topics.description: Understand the opportunities and inequities of English-medium publishing for multilingual scholars: the dominance of English in high-status indexes, the extra time and cost of writing in an additional language, the material constraints faced by scholars outside well-resourced institutions, reviewer and editor attitudes to non-standard English, and the role of literacy brokers such as co-authors, editors, translators and language professionals. Scholars can use this understanding to make informed choices about language, venue, collaboration and support, and to recognise structural barriers as structural rather than personal failings.
masteryEvidence: Explains how indexing, evaluation systems and journal policies create pressure to publish in English and what this means for research in other languages
Identifies the kinds of literacy brokers available to them and the ethical boundaries of each kind of help
Distinguishes reviewer comments about clarity that need action from comments that reflect native-speaker bias, and responds to each appropriately
Makes a reasoned decision about the language and venue for a particular piece of work, including multilingual dissemination
Draws on their multilingual repertoire as a resource in reading, writing and collaborative networks
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give the learner a reviewer comment stating 'the English must be checked by a native speaker' attached to a clear manuscript, and ask how they would respond and what support they might seek. Check whether they separate any genuine clarity issues from bias, respond professionally, and know the legitimate forms of language support and their disclosure requirements.

topics.name: Communicating research beyond academia
topics.description: Communicate research to non-academic audiences such as the public, practitioners, policymakers and industry through lay summaries, blogs, social media, talks, visual summaries and impact case material, adapting content, structure, register and claims to each audience while keeping them accurate. Researchers also plan engagement deliberately, as many funders and evaluation systems expect, and manage the risks of oversimplification and online visibility.
masteryEvidence: Writes a lay summary of their research that a non-specialist reader can restate accurately
Adapts the same finding for two different audiences, such as practitioners and the general public, changing framing, detail and register
Preserves the calibration of claims when simplifying, avoiding causal or certainty inflation
Plans an engagement activity with a stated audience, purpose, channel and indicator of reach or benefit
Manages an online professional presence, such as a profile or social media, in line with institutional guidance
topics.assessmentPrompt: Ask the learner to write a 150-word lay summary of a hedged research finding from their own work, then have a non-specialist peer restate it. Check whether the restatement is accurate, whether jargon has been removed or explained, and whether the hedging of the original claim has survived simplification.

topics.name: Academic CVs and biographical statements
topics.description: Write the self-presentation genres of academic careers: academic CVs, with conventional sections, consistently listed outputs and evidence of research, teaching and service, including the narrative CV formats some funders now use; and short biographical statements for conferences, journals, profiles and applications, often in the third person. Each genre balances self-promotion with modesty according to its conventions, and conventions differ across countries, sectors and career stages. Personal statements for postgraduate study are covered separately.
masteryEvidence: Organises an academic CV with conventional sections in a sensible order for the target post or scheme and formats outputs consistently
Adapts the CV for a specific application by selecting and ordering evidence against its criteria
Writes a 100-word third-person bio that foregrounds current role, research focus and relevant achievements
Adjusts the degree of self-promotion and personal information to the genre and to the national or institutional context
Describes their own contributions to co-authored or collaborative work accurately
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give the learner a CV with sections in an unhelpful order, inconsistently formatted publications and no evidence of teaching or engagement, together with a job, studentship or fellowship advertisement. Ask them to restructure the first page and to write a 60-word bio for the same application. Check whether the order serves the advertisement's criteria, outputs are consistently formatted, contributions are described accurately and the bio is concise and in the expected person.

topics.name: Funding, fellowship and grant applications
topics.description: Write the sections of applications for studentships, travel and small grants and early-career fellowships: the case for support or project description, a lay summary, an impact or pathways-to-benefit statement, a track record or narrative CV, a justification of resources and, where required, a data management plan. Assessors, often from outside the applicant's specialism, read applications against published criteria, so writers argue significance, feasibility and their fit with the scheme explicitly, adapt promotional language to funder norms and follow templates, word limits and eligibility rules exactly. Formats and expectations, including the shift from publication lists to narrative CVs, differ across countries, funders and schemes.
masteryEvidence: Analyses a funding call and its assessment criteria and maps each criterion to a section of the application
Writes a case for support whose aims, methods, timeline and expected outcomes a non-specialist assessor can follow and check against the criteria
Writes a lay summary that states the problem, the work and its likely benefit in plain language without overclaiming
States impact or benefit in terms of specific beneficiaries and routes to them rather than generic claims of importance
Presents a track record or narrative CV that gives evidence of capability relevant to the scheme, including contributions beyond publications
Justifies the requested resources item by item against the planned work
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give the learner the criteria for a small travel or research grant and a 300-word draft case for support that describes the topic at length but does not state aims, plan or benefit. Ask them to revise it to 250 words. Check whether each criterion is addressed explicitly, whether the aims and plan are concrete and feasible, whether benefits are specific, and whether the register suits a non-specialist assessor.

topics.name: Participating in conferences
topics.description: Take part in conferences and research seminars beyond giving a paper: asking concise, relevant questions from the floor, chairing a session by introducing speakers, keeping time and managing discussion, and networking in breaks, poster sessions and online channels, then following up contacts by email. Conference discussion follows conventions of turn allocation, politeness and evaluation that vary across fields, events and formats, including online and hybrid ones, and newcomers can learn them by observation and by preparing reusable moves.
masteryEvidence: Asks a question from the floor that is brief, connects to the talk and makes clear what kind of answer is wanted
Chairs a session by introducing speakers accurately, keeping time, inviting questions fairly and closing discussion politely
Starts and sustains a short professional conversation with a researcher they have not met, describing their own research in one or two sentences
Writes a follow-up email after a conference that reminds the recipient of the context and proposes a specific next step
Participates in online or hybrid sessions using chat, hand-raising and question tools appropriately
topics.assessmentPrompt: Play a three-minute recording, or give a transcript, of part of a research talk and ask the learner to formulate one question from the floor; then role-play a two-minute networking conversation with the speaker afterwards. Check whether the question is concise and linked to the talk, whether the learner introduces their own research clearly and briefly, and whether they propose an appropriate follow-up.

topics.name: Personal statements for postgraduate study and funding
topics.description: Write personal statements, statements of purpose and scholarship essays for applications to master's and doctoral programmes and funding schemes, showing fit with the programme or scheme, academic and professional motivation and capability, each supported by specific evidence, within the stated length and prompts. The genre is promotional and is judged against selection criteria that are often implicit. Expectations differ, for example between research-focused statements of purpose for North American graduate programmes and shorter UK personal statements, and between academic applications and employment applications, which are covered separately.
masteryEvidence: Identifies the explicit and implicit criteria in an application's prompts, programme description and scholarship guidance
Writes a statement in which each claim about motivation or capability is supported by a specific experience, achievement or piece of work
Explains fit with the programme or scheme by referring to its specific features, such as modules, research areas or supervisors
Organises the statement as an argument for admission or funding rather than as a chronological life story
Adjusts length, structure and degree of self-promotion to the target institution and country while keeping claims accurate and their own
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give the learner a programme's selection criteria and a paragraph of a statement made of general claims ('I have always been fascinated by…', 'I am a hard-working and motivated person'). Ask them to rewrite it around one specific experience. Check whether the rewrite addresses a named criterion, supports claims with concrete evidence, explains relevance to the programme and keeps a confident but accurate register.

topics.name: Examiners' reports and thesis corrections
topics.description: Interpret the outcome of a thesis examination and the examiners' reports or lists of required changes (for example minor or major corrections, or revise and resubmit), turn them into a prioritised corrections plan, make and record the changes, and write the response document or corrections table that maps each required change to what was done and where. Writers distinguish required from advisory comments, handle language and presentation corrections (often with editorial help within the institution's rules), communicate with the examiner or committee member who approves the corrections and meet regulatory deadlines. Whether this stage follows a viva, precedes a public defence or follows a written-only examination depends on the system.
masteryEvidence: Explains the examination outcome and the regulations that follow from it, including deadlines and who approves the corrections
Converts examiners' comments into a corrections table that separates required from advisory changes and estimates the work each needs
Makes substantive revisions such as clarifying arguments, adding analysis or reframing claims, not only surface edits
Writes a response for each required change stating what was done and where, quoting new text or giving page references
Identifies and corrects language and presentation errors systematically, using editorial help only within the institution's rules
Writes a polite, specific message to the approving examiner to clarify an ambiguous requirement
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give the learner an anonymised examiners' report extract with five comments of different kinds (a required clarification, an advisory suggestion, a request for additional analysis, a set of typographical errors and an ambiguous comment). Ask them to draft the corrections table and one clarification email. Check whether they distinguish required from advisory changes, plan substantive responses, specify locations and phrase the email clearly and courteously.

topics.name: From thesis to articles
topics.description: Turn thesis chapters into journal articles, or reuse published articles within a thesis: identifying a single publishable argument within the larger thesis, re-scoping it for a target journal's readership, compressing the literature review and methods, rewriting the introduction and contribution for a stand-alone paper, and agreeing authorship with supervisors and collaborators. In both directions writers follow text-recycling, disclosure, copyright and permission rules, for example stating that an article is based on a thesis, citing their own earlier publications and checking publishers' policies on reusing published text.
masteryEvidence: Identifies one argument in a thesis chapter or set of chapters that can stand alone as an article for a named journal
Reduces the thesis literature review and methods to the length and focus a journal article requires while keeping what reviewers need to judge the study
Rewrites the introduction and conclusion so that the contribution is stated for the journal's readers rather than for thesis examiners
Applies the target journal's and institution's rules on text recycling, prior publication of theses and permissions, and discloses the thesis or earlier publication appropriately
Agrees authorship and author order for the article with supervisors and collaborators before submission
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give the learner a 1,500-word section of a thesis literature review and ask them to plan how it would be reduced to about 400 words in an article for a named journal, marking what to keep, cut and reframe. Check whether the plan keeps the sources the article's argument needs, cuts material that served only the thesis examiners and reframes the gap for the journal's readers.

topics.name: Open research practices and statements
topics.description: Understand and write the texts that open-research practices require: preprints and their versions, preregistrations and registered reports, data and code availability statements, data management plans, licence choices, persistent identifiers such as ORCID iDs and data DOIs, and statements that meet funder and institutional open-access and rights-retention requirements. Writers state accurately what is shared, where, under what conditions and why some data cannot be shared, and keep the plan, the preregistration and the final report consistent with each other and with consent documents. Norms differ across disciplines, for example between quantitative and qualitative research, and policies change often, so writers check current requirements.
masteryEvidence: Explains the purpose and limits of preprints, preregistration, registered reports and data sharing in their field
Writes a data availability statement that states what data and code are available, where, under what licence or access conditions, and why any data are restricted
Writes a preregistration or registered-report protocol whose hypotheses, methods and analysis plan are specific enough to be checked, and reports deviations transparently
Completes a data management plan on a funder or institutional template, consistent with the ethics approval and consent documents
Identifies the open-access, licence and rights-retention requirements that apply to their work and states compliance accurately
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give the learner a short study description involving interview data collected under confidentiality commitments, a funder policy requiring data sharing and a draft availability statement that reads 'Data available on request.' Ask them to rewrite the statement. Check whether it specifies what is shared, where and under what conditions, explains the restriction on confidential data and matches the consent terms.

topics.name: IMRaD and its variants
topics.description: Recognise the Introduction–Methods–Results–Discussion macrostructure as a conventional way of reporting empirical research, explain what each section does for the reader, and identify the variants used in one's own field, such as merged Results and Discussion, a separate Conclusions section, a theory section before Methods, or argument-led organisation in the humanities. Knowing the macrostructure lets writers put content where readers expect it, while recognising IMRaD as a disciplinary convention rather than a universal norm.
masteryEvidence: States the communicative purpose of each section of a research article from their own field in one sentence each
Identifies at least two departures from canonical IMRaD in a set of field-specific articles and names the function each variant serves
Relocates misplaced content in a draft, for example interpretation in Methods or new findings in Discussion, and justifies the move by section function
Explains why a theoretical, historical or practice-based paper may not use IMRaD, with reference to how that field makes knowledge claims
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give the learner three short articles from different fields (for example biochemistry, applied linguistics and history) with headings removed. Ask them to mark where each section begins and what it does. Check whether they reason from function (reporting procedure, presenting findings, interpreting) rather than from surface cues, and whether they treat the non-IMRaD article as differently organised rather than defective.

topics.name: Research questions and hypotheses
topics.description: Formulate and present an aim, research questions and, where the design calls for them, hypotheses that are answerable, appropriately scoped and aligned with the stated gap and the chosen methods. Writers also choose how to present them, as numbered questions, objectives or a purpose statement, and use consistent wording across the introduction, methods and discussion. Well-formed questions are the reference point that examiners and reviewers use to judge the coherence of the whole study.
masteryEvidence: Distinguishes an aim, an objective, a research question and a testable hypothesis, and selects the form suited to the design (exploratory, explanatory or confirmatory)
Rewrites a vague or yes/no question into one whose wording specifies population, phenomenon and the kind of answer sought
Checks that each question can be answered by the proposed data and analysis, and revises or drops questions that cannot
Keeps question wording stable across introduction, methods, results and discussion, or signals and justifies any change
Uses hypothesis language accurately, including directional predictions and null hypotheses where the field expects them
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give the learner a one-paragraph study summary with three flawed research questions (one too broad, one yes/no with no analytic purchase, one not answerable from the data described). Ask them to diagnose and rewrite each. Check whether the rewrites are answerable with the described data, and whether the learner explains the misalignment rather than only changing the wording.

topics.name: Establishing a research gap
topics.description: Construct the textual case that a niche exists, through counter-claiming, indicating a gap, raising a question, continuing a tradition or adding to what is known, using the lexicogrammar that realises these moves: contrastive connectors, negative or restrictive quantifiers (few studies, little attention), present perfect for the state of research and evaluative lexis. The niche must follow from the literature reviewed and lead to the present study, and it should be stated with appropriate caution, since an overstated gap ('no research exists') is easily refuted.
masteryEvidence: Identifies the type of niche in published introductions (counter-claim, gap, question, continuation or extension) and the signalling language used
Writes a niche statement that is grounded in specific cited work rather than asserted in general terms
Calibrates gap claims, for example by limiting scope ('in this population', 'longitudinally') rather than claiming that nothing has been done
Links the niche explicitly to the aims or questions of the present study so that the study answers the gap it has opened
Varies niche-establishing resources (adversative connectors, negative quantifiers, contrastive evaluation) rather than relying on one formula
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give the learner a short review paragraph (four or five cited studies) and ask them to write two to three sentences establishing a niche for a stated study. Check whether the gap is traceable to the cited studies, whether its scope is defensible, whether it leads directly to the stated aim, and whether the language is hedged and evaluative rather than absolute.

topics.name: Research article introductions
topics.description: Write research introductions that create a research space: establishing a territory (in Swales's 1990 model by claiming centrality, making topic generalisations and reviewing previous research; in the 2004 revision through cited topic generalisations of increasing specificity), establishing a niche (indicating a gap or adding to what is known), and presenting the present work (the 1990 'occupying the niche'), by announcing the research and its questions and, optionally, its methods, findings, value and structure. Writers adapt the model to their field and genre, including the cyclical moves, extended background and thesis-structure statements common in some disciplines and in PhD introductions, and they use it as an analytical lens on exemplars rather than as a fill-in template.
masteryEvidence: Annotates a published introduction from their own field for moves and steps, including recursive Move 1–Move 2 cycles where present
Writes an introduction in which the territory narrows towards the niche, the niche follows from cited work, and the announcement of the study answers the niche
Decides, with reference to field exemplars, whether to announce principal findings and outline the structure of the text in the introduction
Adapts the move structure for a thesis introduction, including statements of thesis structure, scope and definitions where expected
Explains how their discipline's introductions differ from the canonical CARS model and why
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give the learner a published introduction with its sentences jumbled. Ask them to reconstruct the order and label each sentence by move. Then ask which optional steps the author used and why. Check whether they rely on functional cues (generalisation, contrast, announcement) and whether they can justify optional steps by field convention.

topics.name: Literature review in research writing
topics.description: Write the literature review of a dissertation, thesis or article as an argument that positions the writer's own study: selecting and organising literature by theme, debate or problem, evaluating rather than merely reporting it, and building cumulatively towards the niche the study fills. The research literature review is judged by how well it justifies the present study's questions, framework and design. It is taught to master's dissertation writers and doctoral researchers; the stand-alone literature review assignment set in undergraduate and taught-master's modules is a separate student genre.
masteryEvidence: Organises the review around themes, debates or problems that map onto the study's questions, not around individual sources or chronology by default
Uses citation for a range of functions, including support, comparison, evaluation and application to the writer's own study, not attribution alone
Signals the writer's evaluative stance on bodies of work and individual studies while representing them fairly
Ends sections and the whole review with explicit links to the gap, framework or design of the present study
Justifies inclusion and exclusion of literature and, where relevant, describes how it was located
topics.assessmentPrompt: Ask the learner to bring a draft review section and to state, in one sentence per paragraph, how that paragraph contributes to justifying their study. Check whether every paragraph can be linked to the questions, framework or design, whether the paragraphs contain evaluative commentary, and whether any paragraphs are source-by-source summaries with no positioning.

topics.name: Theoretical and conceptual frameworks
topics.description: Write a theoretical or conceptual framework section that explains which theories, models or concepts the study uses, why they were chosen over alternatives, how key constructs are defined and operationalised, and how the framework shapes the questions, data collection and analysis. The section should do analytical work later in the text rather than function as a free-standing summary of theory, and it should acknowledge disciplinary differences in whether and how frameworks are presented.
masteryEvidence: States which theory or set of concepts frames the study and justifies the choice against at least one plausible alternative
Defines key constructs and shows how each is operationalised or used analytically in the study
Distinguishes, in their own field's terms, between a theoretical framework, a conceptual framework and a literature review
Traces the framework's concepts forward into the analysis and discussion, for example as coding categories, variables or interpretive lenses
Represents theoretical sources accurately while making clear what the writer adopts, adapts or rejects
topics.assessmentPrompt: Ask the learner to explain in two minutes how one named concept from their framework appears in their methods and in their findings. Check whether they can trace the concept into instruments, codes or variables and into interpretation; a learner who can only summarise the theory has written a description, not a framework.

topics.name: Methods sections
topics.description: Write methods sections that describe the study (setting, participants or materials, instruments, procedures, data analysis) in enough detail for evaluation or replication and that establish credibility by justifying choices, citing precedents and addressing validity, reliability or trustworthiness. Move structure, level of detail, voice and the balance of description and justification vary considerably across disciplines and between laboratory, survey and qualitative traditions, so writers calibrate against field exemplars and reporting guidelines (for example CONSORT, STROBE, COREQ or SRQR, collected by the EQUATOR Network).
masteryEvidence: Includes the elements a reader in their field needs to evaluate or replicate the study, checked against an exemplar or reporting guideline
Justifies key design and analysis choices by rationale or precedent rather than only describing them
Orders information so that procedures are traceable, using sub-headings conventional in the field
Chooses voice, tense and agency appropriately, for example past passive or active 'we' for completed procedures and present tense for standard materials, according to field norms
Addresses validity, reliability or trustworthiness, and ethics approval where required, in the conventional place
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give the learner a methods paragraph that describes procedures without any justification. Ask them to identify the two decisions a reviewer would most likely question and to add one justification for each. Check whether they target consequential decisions such as sampling or analysis, and whether the justifications use rationale or cited precedent rather than restating the procedure.

topics.name: Results sections
topics.description: Present findings in a logical order that answers the research questions, using visuals and prose together: locating the reader in a table or figure, highlighting what is significant, and adding the degree of commentary the field allows (from minimal to substantial interpretation). Writers decide what to report in text and what to leave in visuals, separate reporting from interpretation where the genre requires it, and keep claims proportionate to the data.
masteryEvidence: Orders results by research question or by importance rather than in the order the analyses were run
Writes location statements and highlighting statements that select key patterns rather than repeating every value in a table
Adds commentary such as comparison, explanation or evaluation at the level typical of their field's results sections
Uses tense consistently, typically past for findings and present for what a table or figure shows
Keeps claims about results within what the data support, with appropriate hedging where findings are tentative
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give the learner a table with six to eight values and a research question. Ask for a 100-word results paragraph. Check whether they locate the table, select the two or three patterns relevant to the question, avoid restating every number, use tense appropriately and keep any comment proportionate to the data.

topics.name: Reporting quantitative findings
topics.description: Report descriptive and inferential statistics in the conventional format of the field or style guide: test statistics, degrees of freedom, exact p-values (reported as p < .001 when very small), effect sizes and confidence intervals in text and tables, with numbers, symbols and units styled correctly. Writers interpret statistical results in words a reader can follow, distinguish statistical significance from practical importance, and avoid the language of proof or of 'trends towards significance'.
masteryEvidence: Reports a statistical test in the format required by the target style (for example APA) with test statistic, degrees of freedom, p-value and effect size
Accompanies each statistic with a plain-prose statement of what it shows in relation to the research question
Distinguishes statistical significance from the size or practical importance of an effect in the wording of claims
Avoids proof language and dichotomous misreadings of p-values, for example treating p = .06 as 'no effect' or as 'almost significant'
Designs tables with informative titles, notes and units, and does not duplicate table values in prose
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give the learner raw output from a t-test or correlation and ask for one sentence reporting it and one interpreting it. Check the formatting (symbols, italics, decimals, exact p), the presence of an effect size, and whether the interpretation avoids 'proves' and does not equate non-significance with no difference.

topics.name: Reporting qualitative findings
topics.description: Present qualitative findings as an argued interpretation: organising them by theme or category, selecting and introducing participant extracts that illustrate and evidence analytic claims, commenting on each extract, and keeping the analyst's voice distinct from participants' voices. Writers show the range and prevalence of patterns without spurious counting, attend to negative cases, and present extracts ethically and consistently, with pseudonyms, transcription conventions and edits marked. Field notes, analytic memos and accounts of the analysis process are covered by a separate social-science topic.
masteryEvidence: Frames each theme with an analytic claim before presenting supporting extracts, rather than letting quotations carry the argument
Introduces and follows extracts with commentary that explains what the extract shows and how it relates to the theme
Indicates how widespread a pattern is in principled ways and reports disconfirming or divergent cases
Separates participants' accounts from the writer's interpretation through attribution and reporting language
Applies consistent conventions for extract layout, identifiers, omissions and transcription
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give the learner three interview extracts and a theme label. Ask them to write one findings paragraph using two of the extracts. Check whether the paragraph opens with an analytic claim, whether each extract is framed and commented on, whether the analyst's voice is distinguishable from the participants', and whether the choice of extracts is justified.

topics.name: Discussion sections
topics.description: Write discussion sections that move from results to meaning: restating key findings in relation to the research questions, comparing them with previous research, explaining expected and unexpected outcomes, evaluating the study's limitations, and drawing implications. Discussions are typically cyclical, repeating statement–comparison–explanation sequences for each major finding, and their persuasiveness depends on claims calibrated to the evidence and on alternative explanations considered rather than dismissed.
masteryEvidence: Organises the discussion around key findings or research questions, cycling through statement, comparison with literature and explanation for each
Relates each major finding explicitly to cited previous work, stating whether it confirms, extends, qualifies or contradicts it
Offers and weighs more than one possible explanation for unexpected findings
Calibrates the strength of interpretive claims to the design and data, using hedging and boosting deliberately
Draws implications for theory, practice or further research that follow from the findings rather than from the topic in general
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give the learner a results summary with one expected and one unexpected finding and two short abstracts of earlier studies. Ask for a discussion paragraph on the unexpected finding. Check whether they compare it with prior work, propose and evaluate at least two explanations, and hedge appropriately without either overclaiming or retreating into vagueness.

topics.name: Writing about limitations
topics.description: Identify the limitations that genuinely affect how a study's findings can be interpreted (sample, design, measurement, analysis, scope) and write about them so that readers can judge the claims, by stating each limitation, its likely effect on the findings and, where possible, how it was mitigated or could be addressed. Well-written limitations protect the contribution by showing the writer's command of the design, whereas generic or apologetic lists undermine it.
masteryEvidence: Selects limitations that bear on the interpretation of this study's findings rather than listing generic ones such as 'small sample' without consequence
States the likely direction or scope of each limitation's effect on the findings
Pairs limitations with mitigation, counter-weighing strengths or specific future research where justified
Uses concessive and hedging language to acknowledge limitations without retracting the study's main claims
Places limitations where the field expects them, for example in the discussion, a dedicated sub-section or the conclusion
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give the learner a brief study description and a draft limitations paragraph that lists four generic weaknesses and apologises. Ask them to rewrite it. Check whether they keep only consequential limitations, explain how each affects interpretation, add mitigation or a future direction, and avoid both apology and dismissal.

topics.name: Claiming contribution
topics.description: State what the research adds (new evidence, a new method, a new context, a theoretical refinement or a practical application) and why it matters, at a level of confidence the evidence supports. Writers relate the contribution explicitly to the niche established earlier, choose between self-mention and impersonal framing, and balance promotional and cautious language according to field and genre. Doctoral examiners and journal reviewers look for this statement, and its absence or overstatement is a common reason for criticism.
masteryEvidence: States the contribution in one or two sentences that a non-specialist in their department can understand
Classifies the contribution type (empirical, methodological, theoretical, contextual or practical) and words it accordingly
Links the contribution explicitly to the niche established in the introduction or literature review
Calibrates originality claims, avoiding unsupported 'first' and 'novel' claims while not hedging the contribution into invisibility
Uses self-mention or impersonal constructions deliberately, according to field and target genre
topics.assessmentPrompt: Ask the learner to complete the frame 'This study contributes to … by …, which matters because …' for their own project, and then to point to where the matching niche appears in their introduction. Check whether the contribution is specific, of a named type, linked to the niche and calibrated.

topics.name: Conclusions and implications
topics.description: Write concluding sections and chapters that consolidate the research: briefly restating aims and key findings, answering the research questions, articulating the contribution, drawing calibrated implications for theory, practice or policy, evaluating the study and recommending specific further research. In theses, the conclusion also looks across chapters and back to the field, and conventions vary on whether conclusions form a separate section in articles.
masteryEvidence: Answers each research question explicitly in the conclusion, using the same terms as the introduction
Synthesises findings into overall claims rather than repeating chapter summaries
Draws implications that follow from the findings and names who they matter to
Recommends further research with a specific focus and design rather than a generic call
Adjusts length and content to genre: an article conclusion, a dissertation chapter or a thesis conclusion
topics.assessmentPrompt: Ask the learner to read their conclusion alongside their research questions and mark where each question is answered. Then ask them to underline each implication and say which finding it comes from. Check for unanswered questions, implications with no basis in the findings and generic future-research statements.

topics.name: Abstracts for student and research writing
topics.description: Write informative abstracts for student projects, reports, posters and dissertations, and for research articles and theses, that represent the whole work within a tight word limit: typically situating the work, stating its purpose, describing the method, summarising specific results and stating a conclusion or implication, as continuous prose or under the headings of a structured abstract. The same core moves serve both, but student abstracts are judged mainly on accuracy, completeness and concision, whereas research abstracts are also read by searchers and editors as promotional texts whose move emphasis varies across disciplines and journals. Conference abstracts written before results are available are a separate genre.
masteryEvidence: Identifies the moves present and absent in abstracts from their department, programme or target journals
Writes an abstract within a set word limit that includes purpose, method, specific findings and a conclusion or implication in sensible proportion
Reports specific findings rather than promising that results 'will be discussed'
Uses tense and voice consistently with move function and local convention, for example past tense for methods and results and present tense for conclusions
Writes a structured abstract to the required headings when a journal or programme specifies one
Ensures the abstract matches the content and the strength of claims in the full text, without citations or undefined abbreviations unless permitted
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give the learner a 250-word abstract that ends indicatively ('results are discussed') and omits the method, and ask them to rewrite it in 200 words; then ask them to label each sentence by move. Check for an added method, specific findings, a conclusion consistent with those findings, proportionate background and consistent tense.

topics.name: Thesis macrostructure
topics.description: Choose and justify an overall organisation for a dissertation or thesis — traditional simple (IMRaD-like), traditional complex (several studies), topic-based, or publication-based (compilation of articles with framing chapters, assembled during candidature or, in some systems, retrospectively as a PhD by published works), alongside practice-based and professional-doctorate variants that combine an artefact or portfolio with an exegesis or commentary — and plan chapters that fit the research, the institution's regulations and disciplinary norms. Writers understand what each chapter type contributes, how a publication-based thesis builds coherence across stand-alone papers, and what examiners will look for in the whole document.
masteryEvidence: Identifies the macrostructure type of theses from their own department and relates it to the research design
Produces a chapter plan with each chapter's purpose, main claim and approximate length
Explains how their chosen structure presents a coherent argument across the whole document
Weighs a publication-based structure against a monograph for their own project, considering regulations, timing and the status of their papers
Checks the plan against institutional regulations, for example word limits, required elements and rules for including co-authored work
topics.assessmentPrompt: Ask the learner to produce a one-page chapter plan and to explain why they chose this macrostructure rather than one alternative. Check whether the structure fits the design (single study, multiple studies, theory-led or by publication), whether each chapter has a stated purpose and whether regulatory constraints have been checked.

topics.name: Chapter introductions, conclusions and metatext
topics.description: Guide readers through a long document with metatext above the paragraph level: chapter introductions that state purpose and preview structure, chapter conclusions that summarise and link forward, cross-references between chapters, and sign-posting that reminds the reader how the current section serves the thesis argument. Writers calibrate the density of metatext so that it orients the reader without padding or repeating content.
masteryEvidence: Writes chapter introductions that state the chapter's purpose, its relation to the research questions and its structure
Writes chapter conclusions that summarise the chapter's claims and link explicitly to the next chapter
Uses accurate cross-references to other chapters and sections, including forward and backward references
Varies metatext language and keeps it proportionate, avoiding repetitive formulae and preview lists that duplicate headings
Revises metatext after restructuring so that previews and cross-references match the final document
topics.assessmentPrompt: Ask the learner to read only the chapter introductions and conclusions of their draft, in order, to a peer, who then summarises the thesis argument. Check whether the peer can reconstruct the argument, whether chapters link forward and back, and whether any previews or cross-references are inaccurate.

topics.name: Research proposals
topics.description: Write research proposals for admission to doctoral study and for the first-year doctoral plan that persuade reviewers a project is significant, original, feasible and well designed: establishing the problem and gap, stating aims and questions, outlining methods, timeline and resources, anticipating risks and ethics, and articulating expected contributions. Proposals are promissory and evaluative, written in future and conditional terms for readers who must decide quickly. This research genre is distinct from the student project or dissertation proposal written at undergraduate and taught-master's level; later doctoral milestone reports and funding applications have their own topics.
masteryEvidence: Writes a proposal whose aims, questions, methods and expected outcomes align in a way a reviewer can check quickly
Uses future and conditional forms and calibrated promissory language appropriate to work not yet done
Demonstrates feasibility through a realistic timeline, resources and risk-management statements
States the expected contribution in terms that match the institution's or programme's criteria
Adapts structure and emphasis to a specific template, such as a doctoral application form or a departmental proposal guide
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give the learner a doctoral programme's proposal guidelines and assessment criteria and their own 500-word project summary. Ask them to mark where each criterion is addressed and to revise any section that does not address one. Check alignment between aims and methods, evidence of feasibility and whether significance is stated for the specific readers.

topics.name: Ethics applications and participant documents
topics.description: Complete research ethics applications that describe procedures, risks, benefits, consent, confidentiality and data management accurately, and write participant information sheets and consent forms in plain, accessible and, where needed, translated language that enables genuinely informed consent. The genres serve two audiences, the ethics committee and participants, with different register demands, and they commit the researcher to procedures that later methods sections must match.
masteryEvidence: Describes procedures, risks and safeguards in an ethics application completely enough for a committee to assess them
Writes a participant information sheet in plain language, using short sentences, second-person address and no unexplained jargon
Includes the elements participants need, such as purpose, what taking part involves, voluntariness and withdrawal, data use and contacts, following the institution's template
Writes consent statements that are specific, separable where required and unambiguous
Keeps the methods, the ethics application and participant documents consistent with each other
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give the learner a jargon-heavy paragraph from a participant information sheet. Ask them to rewrite it for a lay participant. Check readability (sentence length, terminology, direct address), whether any information has been lost, and whether withdrawal and data-use statements are clear and accurate.

topics.name: Working with supervisors
topics.description: Manage the supervisory relationship through talk and writing: negotiating expectations, preparing agendas and submitting drafts with specific requests for feedback, interpreting and responding to written comments, disagreeing respectfully, and recording decisions and actions after meetings. Supervisory conventions vary across institutions, disciplines and individuals, so learners make these expectations explicit rather than assume them.
masteryEvidence: Discusses and records mutual expectations with the supervisor, for example meeting frequency, turnaround of drafts and type of feedback
Sends drafts with a cover note stating the stage of the draft and two or three specific questions
Prepares a meeting agenda and circulates a short record of decisions and actions afterwards
Interprets indirect feedback comments accurately and responds to each, stating what was changed or why not
Raises disagreement or concerns using mitigated, evidence-based language and knows the institutional routes for unresolved problems
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give the learner three authentic-style supervisor comments, one direct, one hedged ('you might want to consider…') and one cryptic ('?'), and ask what each requires and how they would respond. Check whether they recognise hedged comments as requests and whether they would clarify the cryptic one rather than ignore it.

topics.name: Sustaining thesis writing
topics.description: Sustain writing across a multi-year project by establishing regular, low-stakes writing routines, setting and monitoring realistic writing goals, using writing groups, retreats and accountability partners, separating generative writing from revision, and treating writing as part of doing research rather than as 'writing up' at the end. The aim is steady output and recovery from setbacks without compromising wellbeing.
masteryEvidence: Maintains a writing routine with planned sessions and records output over several weeks
Sets writing goals in terms of specific text, such as section drafts or word counts, rather than vague intentions
Uses at least one social structure for writing, such as a writing group, retreat or accountability partner, and can show from their writing log what it changed in their output
Writes from early in the project (notes, memos, draft sections) instead of postponing writing until the research is finished
Identifies personal patterns of avoidance or over-revision and adjusts strategies in response
topics.assessmentPrompt: Ask the learner to show their writing log or calendar for the last month and to describe what happened in their least productive week. Check whether they have a routine, whether goals are text-specific, and whether they can identify a strategy to try next rather than attributing the problem to motivation alone.

topics.name: Writing positionality statements
topics.description: Write positionality and reflexivity statements that explain how the researcher's identities, experiences, relationships to participants and theoretical commitments may have shaped access, data and interpretation, and what was done about it. Effective statements are analytic and specific to the study rather than confessional or biographical, use first-person reference according to field conventions, and are integrated with methodological decisions rather than isolated in a separate box.
masteryEvidence: Identifies aspects of their own position that plausibly affected this study's access, data or interpretation, and omits those that did not
Explains the likely effect of each aspect and the steps taken to address it, such as memoing, member checking or peer debriefing
Uses first-person reference where the field's exemplars do, consistently across reflexive passages, without retreating into third-person self-reference ('the researcher')
Integrates reflexive comments into methods and discussion where they bear on specific decisions or interpretations
Distinguishes positionality statements from personal narrative or justification of interest in the topic
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give the learner two positionality statements, one listing identity categories without consequence and one linking a specific insider position to access and interpretation. Ask which is more useful to a reader and why, then ask for a three-sentence statement for their own study. Check for specificity, stated consequences and actions taken.

topics.name: Acknowledgements
topics.description: Write the acknowledgements section of dissertations, theses and articles: thanking supervisors, participants, funders, institutions and others in a conventional order and register, including the funding, contribution and competing-interest statements that institutions and journals require, and distinguishing acknowledgement from authorship. In theses it is a short but socially significant part-genre that combines personal gratitude with institutional and ethical obligations; in articles it is brief and formulaic and sits alongside other required declarations.
masteryEvidence: Organises thanks following conventional moves for the genre (for example a reflecting move, thanking moves and an announcing move accepting responsibility)
Includes required elements such as funding sources and grant numbers in the form the institution or journal specifies
Distinguishes contributors who merit acknowledgement from those who meet authorship criteria
Selects a register more personal than the main text but appropriate for a public academic document
Respects participant confidentiality and any agreed anonymity when thanking participants or organisations
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give the learner a list of people and bodies (supervisor, anonymous interview participants, a funder with grant number, a statistician who advised on analysis, a partner, a colleague who proofread). Ask for a 120-word thesis acknowledgement and a two-sentence article acknowledgement. Check ordering, inclusion of the funding detail, protection of anonymity, register, and how contributors are handled relative to authorship.

topics.name: Doctoral progression and confirmation reviews
topics.description: Write the report required at formal doctoral milestones, such as confirmation of candidature, MPhil-to-PhD upgrade or transfer and annual progression review, and discuss it with a review panel. The report typically summarises progress, presents revised questions and design, reports preliminary findings or includes a sample chapter, and sets out a plan, timeline, risks and training needs; the panel judges feasibility, coherence and the candidate's ability to explain and defend choices orally. Names, timings, components and outcomes vary widely across institutions and countries (North American programmes, for example, use qualifying examinations and prospectus defences instead), so local regulations define the genre.
masteryEvidence: Identifies from local regulations the components, length, assessors, criteria and possible outcomes of their own milestone review
Writes a progress report that states what has been done and what has changed since the original proposal, justifying each change with evidence from the work so far
Presents preliminary findings or a draft chapter with claims calibrated to their provisional status
Produces a realistic plan and timeline to submission that names dependencies, risks, mitigation and training or support needs
Explains and defends design decisions in a panel discussion, conceding valid concerns and stating how the plan will respond to them
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give the learner a one-page summary of their progress report and run a ten-minute panel conversation with two questions about feasibility and one about a change of design, each followed by a probing follow-up. Check whether the learner explains what has changed and why, answers feasibility concerns with specific evidence from the plan, concedes genuine risks without abandoning the project and commits to concrete next steps.

topics.name: Thesis by publication
topics.description: Write the integrative texts that turn a set of published, submitted or publishable papers into one examinable thesis: an introductory exegesis that frames the research problem and shows how the papers address it, linking passages or chapter prefaces that explain the progression between papers, a concluding chapter that synthesises findings and states the overall contribution, and statements of the candidate's contribution to co-authored papers. Examiners assess the coherence of the whole, not only the quality of each paper. Rules on the number, status and authorship of papers, word limits and the reproduction of published text vary by institution, discipline and country, and the retrospective PhD by published works, with a critical commentary on earlier publications, is a related variant.
masteryEvidence: Identifies the institutional rules for a thesis by publication, including the number and status of papers, contribution statements, word limits and the format of reproduced articles
Writes an introductory chapter that states the overarching problem, aims and framework and explains how each paper addresses part of it
Writes linking text between papers that explains why each study followed from the previous one and what it adds
Writes a concluding chapter that synthesises findings across papers into an overall contribution rather than summarising each paper in turn
Writes accurate statements of their own contribution to each co-authored paper in the form the institution requires
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give the learner the abstracts of three papers from one doctoral project and ask for a 300-word linking narrative for the thesis introduction. Check whether the narrative states an overarching problem, explains the logical relation between the papers rather than their chronology, identifies what the set contributes together and avoids repeating the abstracts.

topics.name: Writing systematic and scoping reviews
topics.description: Write the protocol and report of a systematic, scoping or other structured review: stating a focused review question, registering or publishing a protocol where the field expects it, reporting search sources, strategies and selection transparently with a flow diagram, describing risk-of-bias or quality appraisal, writing the narrative or quantitative synthesis, and stating conclusions calibrated to the amount and certainty of the evidence. Reporting guidelines such as PRISMA 2020 and its extensions, including PRISMA-ScR for scoping reviews, set readers' expectations. Structured reviews are now common master's and doctoral outputs in health, education, social policy, management, psychology and software engineering, not only in medicine.
masteryEvidence: Distinguishes systematic, scoping and narrative reviews by purpose and method and chooses the type that fits the review question
Writes a review question and eligibility criteria using a framework suited to the field, such as population, concept and context
Reports search sources, full search strategies, dates and selection procedures so that a reader could repeat them, including a flow diagram with numbers at each stage
Describes how included studies were appraised and uses the appraisal in the synthesis rather than reporting it separately
Writes a synthesis organised by findings or themes across studies, not study by study
Calibrates conclusions to the number, quality and consistency of included studies and states the review's own limitations
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give the learner a methods section from a published review with the search and selection details removed, together with the PRISMA 2020 checklist items for those sections. Ask them to list what is missing and to draft the missing sentences for a stated search. Check whether they include sources, dates, availability of the full strategy, the screening procedure and numbers, in precise past-tense prose.

topics.name: Wording survey and interview questions
topics.description: Write questionnaire items, response scales and interview prompts that participants can understand and answer as intended: one idea per item, neutral rather than leading wording, no unexplained jargon or double negatives, response options that are balanced, exhaustive and non-overlapping, and open interview prompts with planned follow-up probes. Writers pilot the instrument with people like the intended participants, check how items are understood and revise; where participants use other languages, translation and checking with fluent speakers are part of the wording process. Badly worded items produce data that later analysis cannot repair.
masteryEvidence: Rewrites double-barrelled, leading, presupposing, negatively worded and jargon-laden items as single-focus, neutral items
Designs response scales whose options are balanced, mutually exclusive and exhaustive, with labelled points and a justified decision about a midpoint or 'not applicable' option
Writes open interview prompts and follow-up probes that invite description and examples rather than yes/no answers or agreement
Links each item or prompt to a research question or construct and removes items that serve none
Pilots the instrument with people similar to the intended participants, records how items were interpreted and revises in response
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give the learner five flawed questionnaire items (one double-barrelled, one leading, one with a double negative, one with overlapping response options and one with undefined jargon) and ask them to diagnose and rewrite each. Check whether each rewrite asks one thing neutrally in language the stated participants would understand, and whether the response options now cover all answers without overlap.

topics.name: Teaching, demonstrating and marking as a doctoral researcher
topics.description: Communicate as a graduate teaching assistant, tutor or demonstrator: explaining concepts and procedures to undergraduates at an appropriate level, asking and handling questions, managing small-group discussion, giving clear practical or laboratory instructions including safety information, and writing feedback on student work that is specific, criterion-referenced and consistent with the module's marking guidance. Many institutions screen or train international teaching assistants' spoken English, but how well students understand also depends on organisation, checks of understanding and listeners' expectations, so the topic treats teaching communication as shared and learnable rather than as an accent problem.
masteryEvidence: Explains a key concept or procedure from their field to undergraduates using a clear structure, examples and checks of understanding
Asks open and follow-up questions that draw out student reasoning, and responds to student questions by clarifying, answering or redirecting them to the group
Gives practical or laboratory instructions, including safety points, in a sequence students can follow, and confirms that they have been understood
Writes feedback on a student assignment that refers to the marking criteria, identifies strengths and priorities and suggests specific next steps
Manages a small-group discussion so that several students contribute, using fair turn allocation and accepting different modes of participation
Handles a student query about marks or deadlines politely and within their role, referring it to the module leader where appropriate
topics.assessmentPrompt: Ask the learner to give a five-minute explanation of a concept from a first-year module in their field to two or three peers acting as students, each of whom asks one clarification question. Then give them a short student answer with the marking criteria and ask for three sentences of written feedback. Check the structure and level of the explanation, how questions are handled, whether understanding is checked, and whether the feedback is criterion-referenced and actionable.

dependencies.reason: Understanding the publishing process as an author builds on the reader-side knowledge of how peer review, journals and other scholarly outputs work
Editorial screening, corrections and retractions are integrity mechanisms that are best understood once research integrity has been introduced
