Comparing journals on review practices, turnaround and article types requires knowing how the process works
Screening out predatory and deceptive venues depends on recognising their characteristics
Judging fit requires a clear statement of what the manuscript contributes and to whom
A cover letter argues fit with a specific journal, which must already be chosen and analysed
Formal academic correspondence conventions (salutation, purpose, closing) are first learned in emails to staff
Declarations of originality and no simultaneous submission depend on understanding the rules on reusing one's own work
Responding appropriately requires understanding decision types and the roles of editors and reviewers
Disagreeing with gatekeepers while remaining cooperative depends on control of face and politeness strategies
Partial acceptance and reasoned rebuttal of reviewer points use concessive and counter-argument language
Translating reviewer comments into a revision plan extends the habit of acting on feedback
Evaluating a manuscript's validity depends on critical reading of samples, design and measures
Constructive reviewing relies on praise–criticism pairs and mitigated critique
Reviewers need to understand their role, the editor's needs and the meaning of recommendations
Classroom peer review of drafts is usually the first experience of giving structured written feedback
Conference abstracts adapt the move structure of research abstracts to a call for papers
Reporting expected or preliminary results requires predictive and speculative language
A viva is extended question handling, which requires clarifying, answering, deferring and managing difficult questions
Defending a thesis requires constructing and sustaining arguments in real-time spoken interaction
Examiners routinely ask candidates to state and defend their contribution to knowledge
Conceding limitations without undermining the thesis is a recurrent viva demand
General preparation and performance strategies for oral assessment are usually met before the doctoral viva
Authorship criteria and contribution statements are defined within journal publication processes
Experience of co-authoring workflows grounds discussion of who qualifies as an author
Documenting one's own and others' roles in group work prepares learners for contributor-role statements
Analysing inequities in publishing requires knowing how the process and its gatekeeping work
Recognising native-speaker bias in review builds on questioning native-speaker norms as the benchmark
Engagement writing applies plain-language principles and public registers to one's own research
Researchers must be able to state their contribution clearly before translating it for other audiences
Social media engagement depends on norms for professional online presence and privacy
Visual summaries are a common engagement format and draw on infographic design
Self-presentation genres require deliberate choices about first- and third-person self-reference and authorial roles
Presenting oneself as a scholar draws on awareness of how writing constructs academic identity
Publication lists on CVs follow reference-list conventions consistently
Learners need experience of reading research articles section by section before they can analyse the macrostructure as a writer
Seeing IMRaD as a conventional, community-shaped response to recurring purposes depends on the concept of genre and discourse community
Explaining why fields depart from IMRaD requires understanding that disciplines differ in what counts as knowledge and evidence
Formulating research questions for a study builds on the prior skill of narrowing a topic into a focused, searchable question
Research questions are usually motivated by unresolved or contested points identified across the literature
Stating hypotheses and predictions uses the speculative and predictive language taught under hypothesising
A writer must first identify what is unresolved or under-researched before constructing a textual niche around it
Counter-claiming and indicating limitations in prior work use the language of mitigated evaluation of others' research
Gap statements rely on tense choices, especially present perfect for the state of research, to represent the field as currently incomplete
Establishing a niche is the pivotal move of a CARS introduction and must be controlled before the full move sequence can be written
Occupying the niche requires announcing aims and questions, which must already be formulated
Knowing what the introduction must set up for later sections helps writers decide what belongs in it
Learners usually meet general-to-specific essay introductions first, and CARS is taught as a research-genre extension of that movement
A research literature review is built from paragraphs that put multiple sources in dialogue around a point
Organising a review by themes and debates requires a prior map of the field's themes, key authors and schools of thought
The research review is judged by how well it builds towards a niche, so niche construction must be controlled
Coursework literature reviews usually come first and provide the thematic-synthesis base that positioning a study extends
Positioning a study depends on using citation for evaluation, comparison and application, not attribution alone
A framework section shows how concepts will be used to analyse data, which presupposes the ability to apply theory to a case
Framework sections define and operationalise contested constructs, a skill developed in work with concepts
Choosing and justifying a framework draws on the review of how others have theorised the problem
Writers need to know what the methods section does within the macrostructure, and what it does not do, before drafting it
Describing procedures depends on sequencing, purpose expressions and passive constructions taught under describing processes
Results prose is built from location, highlighting and commentary statements, the core of data commentary
Deciding how much interpretation belongs in Results rather than Discussion depends on understanding section functions
Writers cannot report p-values, effect sizes and confidence intervals accurately without being able to interpret them
Statistical reporting conventions are applied within the organisation and commentary of a results section
Statistical prose applies style-guide rules for numerals, symbols, decimals and units
Qualitative findings sections share the results genre's logic of ordering findings by question and adding commentary, even when merged with discussion
Presenting participant extracts uses the same framing, grammatical integration and commentary skills as integrating source quotations
Keeping analyst interpretation distinct from participants' accounts depends on tracking averral and attribution
A discussion interprets findings already reported, and writers need to separate the two functions
Comparing one's findings with prior studies uses the language of agreement, extension and qualification across sources
Accounting for expected and unexpected findings requires language for reasons, mechanisms and rationales
Evaluating the study is a typical discussion move, so writing limitations is usually taught as a component before the whole section
Identifying consequential limitations in one's own study requires the ability to evaluate samples, designs and measures critically
Limitations are stated relative to the design and procedures described in the methods section
Acknowledging limitations while maintaining claims uses concessive constructions (although, admittedly, nevertheless)
A contribution is defined relative to the niche the writer has established, so niche construction comes first
Originality and significance claims must be matched to what the evidence and design support
Contribution statements commonly use self-mention to mark the writer's own role and originality
Conclusions consolidate interpretations, implications and evaluation already developed in the discussion
Articulating the contribution is a central move in research conclusions
Implications for practice and recommendations for further research use recommending language
Learners usually meet essay conclusions first, and research conclusions extend that synthesising function
Abstract moves map onto the sections of the full text, so knowledge of the macrostructure is needed to condense it
Research abstracts must state what the study adds, which depends on having articulated the contribution
Empirical theses often adapt IMRaD, although topic-based, theoretical and humanities theses do not
Experience of the taught-programme dissertation is usually the starting point for planning a thesis
Planning a publication-based thesis requires understanding how articles are submitted, reviewed and published
Chapter-level metatext guides readers through a planned macrostructure; master's dissertation chapters can be signposted before thesis planning is taught
Chapter previews and cross-references extend text-level frame markers and advance organisers to the scale of a thesis
Linking chapters applies the bridging techniques used between paragraphs and sections
Chapter conclusions use the language of summarising and drawing conclusions
A proposal is built around aims and questions that must be formulated and scoped
Proposals must position the project in the literature and justify the gap in condensed form
Proposed methods are written using the same content and justification conventions as methods sections, recast in the future tense
Expected significance and contribution are central evaluation criteria for proposals
Student project proposals are usually written first and introduce the rationale–aims–methods–timeline structure
Ethics applications presuppose understanding of research integrity, data management and responsible conduct
Participant information sheets must be written in plain language for lay readers
Ethics applications require clear sequential descriptions of procedures participants will experience
Participant-facing documents must refer to groups and individuals respectfully and inclusively
Productive supervision depends on requesting targeted feedback on drafts
Supervision meetings extend the preparation and interaction skills of one-to-one tutorials
Agendas, decision records and action points are first practised in group meetings
Sustaining thesis writing extends scheduling, milestone and word-count planning for extended projects
Generative writing and lowering perfectionism are core tools for sustained output
Long-term productivity depends on sustainable workload and stress management
Writing positionality statements requires prior understanding of reflexivity and how position shapes interpretation
Positionality statements depend on confident, appropriate first-person self-mention
Choosing how visible to make the researcher in different parts of a text draws on understanding of impersonality and authorial presence
Reflexive comments are integrated with methodological decisions described in the methods section
Interpreting findings, comparing them with prior work and proposing explanations requires matching each claim's strength to what the results can support
Stating limitations is the counterpart of calibrating claims: it marks the scope beyond which the study's claims should not be extended
Methods sections force the choice between agentless passives and author-visible 'we' or 'I'; learners need the impersonality-presence choice to make it deliberately
Acknowledgements are part of the dissertation's front matter, and their conventions and placement follow from the overall structure of the document
Article acknowledgements list contributors who do not meet authorship criteria, so deciding who is acknowledged depends on knowing those criteria
An abstract condenses a whole text to its essential content within a strict word limit.
Abstracts shift between present and past tense according to move, which draws on tense choices for reporting research.
Word limits make concise phrasing essential to include all required moves.
The progress report revisits and revises the aims, questions, methods and plan first set out in the doctoral proposal
The oral review requires answering and following up panel questions about the design
Many panels begin with a short presentation of the project and its preliminary findings
Reports are drafted with and usually endorsed by the supervisory team, so negotiating feedback on drafts comes first
Choosing and planning a publication-based thesis depends on knowing the range of thesis structures and what each chapter type contributes
Contribution statements for co-authored papers apply authorship criteria and contributor roles
Linking narratives and chapter prefaces are higher-level metatext that guides examiners across separately written papers
Reproducing published papers in a thesis raises the text-reuse, copyright and disclosure questions covered by reusing one's own work
Reporting a review search transparently depends on having designed and recorded a systematic search
The protocol and methods of a review apply methods-section conventions: complete, ordered and justified procedures
Reporting risk-of-bias assessment and weighting evidence in a synthesis builds on appraising single studies
Synthesising across studies and positioning the review build on writing a literature review as an argument
Items and prompts operationalise the research questions, so they cannot be written or checked without them
Turning concepts into indicators that can be measured or asked about comes before wording individual items
Neutral, bias-free item wording applies inclusive-language principles to research participants
Teaching undergraduates rests on explaining concepts and readings clearly to others
Managing small-group discussion as a tutor extends facilitation skills developed in peer seminars
Responding to student questions in class draws on handling audience questions
Criterion-referenced feedback on student work requires interpreting marking criteria from the marker's side
The case for support applies the proposal genre's alignment of aims, methods, timeline and expected contribution to a funder's template
Lay summaries and impact statements draw on adapting research for non-academic audiences and planning engagement
Track-record sections and narrative CVs build on academic CV and self-presentation conventions
Many funders require data management plans and open-access commitments written to open-research conventions
Asking questions from the floor extends asking questions and seeking clarification in seminars
Conference discussion includes answering questions on one's own work and knowing how question sessions run
Participating in conferences usually accompanies presenting one's own research
Networking at conferences builds on informal interaction and small talk with academics
Every claim about motivation and capability must be supported with specific evidence
Statements are shaped by the selectors' purposes and criteria
Presenting oneself as a prospective postgraduate draws on understanding academic and writer identity
First-person self-presentation requires deliberate control of self-mention
Planning and making corrections applies the processes of interpreting and acting on feedback to examiners' reports
In many systems corrections follow the viva, whose outcome and discussion define what must change
A corrections table follows the point-by-point, traceable conventions of responses to journal reviewers
Language corrections often involve editorial help whose acceptable limits must be known
Re-scoping a chapter as an article requires understanding how the thesis distributes its argument across chapters
Reframing thesis material depends on a chosen target journal's readership and conventions
Moving text between a thesis and articles applies text-recycling and disclosure rules
Articles from a thesis require authorship decisions with supervisors and collaborators
Open-research statements are integrity commitments about transparency, data and disclosure
Preprints, registered reports and availability statements are stages and requirements of the publication process
Writing open-access and licence statements builds on understanding open access from the reader's side
Data-sharing statements and data management plans must be consistent with consent and ethics commitments
The confirmation or progression panel is usually the candidate's first oral defence of the research and rehearses the explaining, defending and conceding moves of the viva
Cover letters must make the data-availability, preregistration and preprint declarations that open-research practices generate
Navigating English-medium publishing as a multilingual scholar draws on a critical understanding of whose norms are rewarded
Reviewer confidentiality includes not exposing manuscripts to AI tools, which builds on understanding the privacy and intellectual-property risks of AI
Thanking participants and sites without breaching anonymity depends on the confidentiality commitments made in ethics documents
Positioning a study within literature involves deliberate choices about whose work is cited
Publishing as a multilingual scholar includes deciding when translingual choices are viable

guidance.summary: Novice authors often see publication as a single gate rather than a negotiated process. Gosden (1995) traced how novice researchers' articles changed through review and revision, and Myers (1990) showed claims being renegotiated between authors and reviewers, both supporting a view of publication as social negotiation within a discourse community. W. L. Belcher (2019) gives practical guidance on interpreting journal decisions, and Lillis and Curry (2010) show that publication involves networks of people beyond the named authors. Teach the process with authentic decision letters and reviews where possible, since these genres are rarely visible to novices.

activities.title: Decision letter decoding
learnerActions: Read three anonymised decision letters (minor revision, major revision, reject and resubmit)
Identify what the editor is asking for and the deadline in each
Classify reviewer comments as essential, negotiable or optional
Plan the next steps for one letter, with a timeline
activities.intendedInsight: Most first decisions are invitations to revise, and editors' letters signal which comments matter most.
activities.rationale: Revision in response to review is central to publication success (Gosden 1995); W. L. Belcher (2019) provides practical guidance on interpreting decisions.

activities.title: Tracing a paper's history
learnerActions: Find an article in your field with published peer review history or open reviews
Compare the submitted and published versions, or the reviews and the final text
Identify changes to claims, structure and hedging
Discuss what the changes reveal about the negotiation between authors and reviewers
activities.intendedInsight: Published articles are the product of negotiation, and claims often change during review.
activities.rationale: Myers (1990) showed claims being renegotiated through review; open peer review now makes this process visible in some journals.

difficulties.pattern: My paper was rejected, so my research is worthless.
difficulties.revealedBy: Abandoning papers after a first rejection or after a major-revision decision misread as rejection.
difficulties.response: Normalise rejection and revision with examples, including supervisors' own experience where they are willing to share it, and plan resubmission strategies.

difficulties.pattern: Peer review is an objective quality check, so the reviewers must be right.
difficulties.revealedBy: Uncritical acceptance of all reviewer comments, including contradictory ones.
difficulties.response: Discuss review as expert judgement exercised by individuals, with variability and bias, and the editor's role in adjudicating.

diagnostic.task: Ask the learner to explain what happens between submitting a paper and seeing it published in their field, and what they would do after a 'major revision' decision.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Describes the stages and roles accurately, including field-specific features, and treats major revision as an invitation with a clear plan.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Describes the stages broadly but misinterprets decision types or roles.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Has little idea of the process or equates any request for revision with rejection.

guidance.contextNotes: At PGT the topic is introductory, for students who may publish from dissertations or move to doctoral study. At PGR it is core, especially where publication during candidature is expected or the thesis is publication-based.

guidance.summary: Journal selection is best done before drafting, because the target journal shapes the conversation the paper joins, its length, structure and audience. W. L. Belcher (2019) offers a structured approach to identifying and evaluating suitable journals, and Thomson and Kamler (2013) frame journals as discourse communities whose recent content the writer should read and engage with. Lillis and Curry (2010) show that multilingual scholars make venue decisions under institutional incentives that favour English-medium indexed journals. Teaching should combine analysis of recent journal content with critical screening of venues.

activities.title: Journal profile
learnerActions: Choose three candidate journals
For each, record aims and scope, article types, word limits, recent topics, review model, open-access options and indexing
Read the abstracts of the last two issues and note which conversations your paper would join
Rank the journals and justify the ranking to a peer
activities.intendedInsight: Fit depends on the conversation a journal is currently hosting, not just its stated scope or prestige.
activities.rationale: W. L. Belcher (2019) and Thomson and Kamler (2013) both recommend close reading of a journal's recent content as part of choosing it.

activities.title: Venue verification
learnerActions: Examine a journal that has sent you an unsolicited invitation
Check its indexing claims, editorial board, publisher membership of recognised bodies and fee transparency
Compare it with a reputable journal in your field
Write a short verdict with evidence
activities.intendedInsight: Predatory venues can look legitimate, so claims must be verified independently.
activities.rationale: Lateral verification of claims applies information-literacy skills to publishing decisions; the activity is a practical proposal.

difficulties.pattern: I will write the paper first and then look for a journal with the highest impact factor.
difficulties.revealedBy: Manuscripts that do not engage with the target journal's literature, and desk rejections for poor fit.
difficulties.response: Reverse the sequence: choose and analyse journals early and draft with the target journal's readers in mind. Discuss the limits of impact factor as a criterion.

difficulties.pattern: The journal invited me personally and promises publication in two weeks, so it must be good.
difficulties.revealedBy: Submissions to predatory venues, often under pressure to publish quickly.
difficulties.response: Teach verification steps and discuss the career and integrity consequences of predatory publication without shaming those who have been targeted.

diagnostic.task: Ask the learner to name their target journal and explain why it suits their paper.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Justifies the choice by scope, audience, recent content and practical factors, and names alternatives.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Justifies the choice mainly by prestige or by a supervisor's suggestion, with limited analysis of fit.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Has no target journal or cannot explain the choice.

guidance.contextNotes: This topic is primarily for PGR, especially where publication is expected during candidature. Choices are shaped by field norms (journals, conferences or monographs), institutional incentives and funder open-access requirements.

guidance.summary: Swales (1996) characterised the submission letter as an occluded genre, one that is important but rarely visible to novices because such letters are not published. Swales (2004) places such genres within the network of genres that surround research articles. W. L. Belcher (2019) gives practical guidance on what editors look for. Because exemplars are scarce, teachers should collect anonymised letters, with permission, and analyse them alongside journal instructions.

activities.title: Letter anatomy
learnerActions: Analyse two or three anonymised cover letters and the journal instructions they responded to
Identify the moves: identification, contribution, fit, declarations, closing
Note length, register and how fit is argued
Draft a letter for your own manuscript
activities.intendedInsight: Effective cover letters are brief and specific, and they argue fit, which an abstract does not do.
activities.rationale: Making occluded genres visible through exemplars addresses the access problem Swales (1996) identified.

activities.title: Editor's two-minute read
learnerActions: Exchange cover letters with a peer who role-plays a busy editor
The peer reads for two minutes and decides whether to send the paper for review, giving reasons
Revise based on what the editor did or did not notice
activities.intendedInsight: Editors read quickly, so contribution and fit must be immediately visible.
activities.rationale: Role-play makes the reader's constraints concrete; the activity is a proposal informed by W. L. Belcher's (2019) advice on editors' priorities.

difficulties.pattern: Opening with several lines of courtesy formulae and expressions of humility before saying what the manuscript is.
difficulties.revealedBy: Letters whose first paragraph contains courtesy formulae but no title, contribution or fit, often following formal-letter conventions taught at school or used in other varieties of English.
difficulties.response: Show that in English-medium journal correspondence, professional respect is conveyed through concision and specificity rather than honorifics. Present this as a convention of this genre, not as a judgement of other norms; such formulae are standard and respectful in many Englishes and need not be 'corrected' elsewhere.

difficulties.pattern: The cover letter is a formality, so I paste my abstract.
difficulties.revealedBy: Letters that repeat the abstract and do not argue fit with the journal.
difficulties.response: Contrast the purposes of the abstract (summarise for readers) and the cover letter (argue fit for the editor).

diagnostic.task: Ask the learner to tell you in thirty seconds why their manuscript belongs in their target journal.
diagnostic.strongResponse: States the contribution and links it specifically to the journal's scope, readers or recent content.
diagnostic.partialResponse: States the contribution but links it to the journal only generically.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Summarises the paper without addressing fit.

guidance.contextNotes: This is a PGR topic, best taught close to first submission. Some journals now use submission forms rather than letters, but the fit argument usually appears somewhere, and the declarations increasingly include data availability, preregistration, preprint and AI-use statements.

guidance.summary: Responses to reviewers are face-sensitive: authors must comply with or resist gatekeepers' requests while preserving goodwill, which makes Brown and Levinson's (1987) account of face-threatening acts and mitigation a useful lens. Gosden (1995) showed how revision in response to review shaped the success of novice researchers' articles, and Paltridge (2017) analyses the discourse of peer review, including how reviewers frame requests. W. L. Belcher (2019) offers practical formats. Teach a clear point-by-point structure and graded strategies for agreeing, partly agreeing and disagreeing.

activities.title: Response matrix
learnerActions: Paste each reviewer comment into a table
Classify each as agree and revise, partly agree, clarify a misreading or decline with reasons
Draft a response and specify the change (page and line, or quoted new text)
Check that the manuscript changes match the responses
activities.intendedInsight: A systematic structure makes it easy for editors to verify that every point has been addressed.
activities.rationale: W. L. Belcher (2019) recommends point-by-point responses; a matrix links each response to a verifiable change.

activities.title: Disagreeing with gatekeepers
learnerActions: Read three versions of a response declining a reviewer's request: defensive, capitulating and reasoned
Identify the politeness and stance strategies in each
Write a reasoned response to a request from your own reviews that you disagree with
Peer review for tone and evidence
activities.intendedInsight: Disagreement can be accepted by editors when it is reasoned, evidenced and mitigated.
activities.rationale: Brown and Levinson's (1987) framework explains why mitigation and appreciation protect face when disagreeing.

difficulties.pattern: The reviewer is wrong and clearly did not read the paper carefully.
difficulties.revealedBy: Defensive or sarcastic drafts, and blaming the reviewer for misunderstandings.
difficulties.response: Encourage the learner to treat misreadings as evidence that the text was unclear and to revise to prevent them. Suggest a cooling-off period before drafting.

difficulties.pattern: I must accept every comment or the paper will be rejected.
difficulties.revealedBy: Contradictory revisions made to satisfy conflicting reviewers, and changes that weaken the paper.
difficulties.response: Explain that editors expect reasoned disagreement where it is warranted and decide between conflicting reviewers, and model polite declines supported by evidence.

difficulties.pattern: Responses such as 'Done' or 'We have revised accordingly' with no detail.
difficulties.revealedBy: Responses that do not tell the editor what changed or where.
difficulties.response: Require quoted changes or page and line references for every response.

diagnostic.task: Give the learner a reviewer comment requesting an additional analysis that is not feasible, and ask them to draft the response.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Thanks the reviewer, explains why the analysis is not feasible, offers an alternative such as a limitation statement or a sensitivity check, and indicates where the text was changed.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Declines politely but without evidence or an alternative.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Is defensive, ignores the comment or promises an analysis that cannot be done.

guidance.contextNotes: This is a PGR topic. Supervisors and co-authors are often closely involved, so teaching can use real reviews (with permission) and joint drafting.

guidance.summary: Reviewing is both an evaluative genre and an ethical role. The ICMJE recommendations (ICMJE 2025) set out reviewers' responsibilities, including confidentiality and declaring competing interests; journals and funders increasingly state that confidentiality rules out uploading manuscripts to generative AI tools. Paltridge (2017) and Fortanet (2008) analyse the language of referee reports, including how criticism and recommendations are framed. In classroom settings, Lundstrom and Baker (2009) found that L2 writers who gave peer feedback improved their own writing more than those who only received it, which suggests reviewing can also benefit early-career researchers' writing, although that study did not involve journal reviewing.

activities.title: Report structure from exemplars
learnerActions: Read two published (open) review reports from your field
Identify the summary, major concerns, minor points and recommendation
Note how criticism is mitigated and made actionable
Draft a report on a short paper using the same structure
activities.intendedInsight: Useful reports are structured, prioritised and actionable.
activities.rationale: Analysis of referee-report language (Paltridge 2017; Fortanet 2008) provides models of how criticism is framed in this genre.

activities.title: Mock review panel
learnerActions: Review the same short manuscript individually
Compare recommendations and major concerns in a group
Discuss reasons for disagreement and how an editor would adjudicate
Revise your report in light of the discussion
activities.intendedInsight: Reviewers vary, and good reports make their reasoning transparent for the editor.
activities.rationale: Giving feedback can benefit the giver's own writing (Lundstrom & Baker 2009); comparing reviews also reveals variability in judgement.

difficulties.pattern: Reviewing means finding everything wrong with the paper.
difficulties.revealedBy: Long lists of criticisms with no summary, no acknowledgement of strengths and no prioritisation.
difficulties.response: Require a summary and a statement of strengths first, and a separation of major from minor points.

difficulties.pattern: I uploaded the manuscript to an AI tool to summarise it and polish my report.
difficulties.revealedBy: Reviewers unaware of confidentiality rules, and reports with generated summaries that misrepresent the manuscript.
difficulties.response: Explain that manuscripts under review are confidential and that many journals, publishers and funders prohibit uploading them to generative AI tools unless their policy explicitly allows it; check the journal's policy and declare any permitted use. Suggest language support that does not expose the manuscript, such as drafting in the reviewer's stronger language and editing their own text. Involving a co-reviewer, such as a supervisor, also needs the editor's permission.

diagnostic.task: Give the learner a short methods and results extract with a flaw, and ask for the opening summary and one major comment.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Summarises fairly and identifies the flaw as major, explaining its consequences and suggesting a remedy.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Identifies the flaw but frames it vaguely or as minor, or omits the summary.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Misses the flaw or focuses only on language and formatting.

guidance.contextNotes: PGR learners are increasingly invited to review, sometimes alongside supervisors. Conference reviewing, with shorter reports and scoring forms, is a common first experience in computing and engineering.

guidance.summary: Conference abstracts are selection documents read by programme committees, often written before results are available. Swales and Feak (2009) treat conference abstracts as a distinct type, with greater emphasis on interest and promotion than article abstracts, and Halleck and Connor (2006) analysed the rhetorical moves of conference proposals, showing their promotional character. Teach learners to read the call for papers as an assessment brief and to handle incomplete results honestly.

activities.title: Call-for-papers analysis
learnerActions: Read a real call for papers and highlight theme, strands, criteria and requirements
Draft your abstract with explicit reference to the theme
Ask a peer to score it against the call's criteria
activities.intendedInsight: A call for papers is an assessment brief, and abstracts are scored for relevance and interest.
activities.rationale: Conference abstracts differ from article abstracts in purpose and readership (Swales & Feak 2009).

activities.title: Writing ahead of results
learnerActions: Collect accepted abstracts from a past conference that report work in progress
Identify how they present preliminary or expected findings (tense, hedges, 'will discuss')
Write your abstract with an honest treatment of the stage your work has reached
activities.intendedInsight: Reviewers accept work in progress if the claims are honest and the interest is clear.
activities.rationale: Conference proposals have a promotional, forward-looking character (Halleck & Connor 2006) that must be balanced with honesty about results.

difficulties.pattern: I paste my article abstract and cut it to the word limit.
difficulties.revealedBy: Abstracts with no link to the conference theme and no signal of interest to attendees.
difficulties.response: Contrast article and conference abstracts and require explicit reference to the theme.

difficulties.pattern: Results show that… (when data collection has not started).
difficulties.revealedBy: Past-tense results statements for work not yet done.
difficulties.response: Practise future and hedged formulations and discuss the integrity implications of reporting results that do not exist.

diagnostic.task: Give the learner a call for papers and ask how their research could be framed for it, in two minutes.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Links the research to the theme specifically, identifies the likely interest to attendees and is honest about results.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Describes the research accurately but links it to the theme only generically.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Describes the research without reference to the call.

guidance.contextNotes: PGT students may submit to student or practitioner conferences. PGR learners submit to disciplinary conferences, where in some fields, such as computer science, full conference papers are the primary publication venue and the 'abstract' is a different genre.

guidance.summary: The oral examination of a thesis varies across countries and institutions in format, audience, length and outcomes, so the first teaching step is making the local format explicit. Paltridge and Starfield (2020) discuss the examination of the thesis, Tinkler and Jackson (2004) describe the UK doctoral examination process, Swales (2004) discusses the PhD defence as a research genre, and the Routledge handbook of EAP (Hyland & Shaw 2016) includes a review of research on defences and vivas. Preparation should include strategic rereading, anticipating typical question areas such as contribution, methods, findings, limitations and future work, rehearsing extended answers in mock vivas with probing follow-up questions, and understanding what happens after the oral.

activities.title: Mock viva with debrief
learnerActions: Prepare a two-to-three-minute summary of your thesis and its contribution
Take part in a 30-minute mock viva with two colleagues acting as examiners
Review a recording or notes, identifying questions you answered well and those you struggled with
Plan targeted preparation for the struggling areas
activities.intendedInsight: Rehearsal reveals gaps in the oral defence of the thesis that rereading alone does not.
activities.rationale: Mock vivas are widely recommended in doctoral guidance (Tinkler & Jackson 2004; Paltridge & Starfield 2020); evidence on their effectiveness is largely experiential rather than experimental.

activities.title: Answer structures
learnerActions: List likely challenging questions about your thesis
Practise answers that clarify the question, answer directly, support with reference to the thesis and acknowledge limits
Practise conceding a point while maintaining your main claim
Practise asking for clarification and taking time to think
activities.intendedInsight: Structured, direct answers that refer to the thesis are more convincing than long, defensive responses.
activities.rationale: The viva combines extended explanation and argument in interaction; practising answer structures targets both.

difficulties.pattern: The viva is an exam to catch me out, so I must defend every point to the end.
difficulties.revealedBy: Defensive answers, refusal to concede minor points and visible anxiety in mock vivas.
difficulties.response: Present the viva as a scholarly conversation and show how conceding limitations demonstrates mastery. Do not dismiss anxiety; signpost support services where needed.

difficulties.pattern: I answer every question at length and drift away from the question.
difficulties.revealedBy: Long, unfocused answers in mock vivas, and examiners repeating questions.
difficulties.response: Practise answer-first structures and brief checks ('Does that answer your question?').

difficulties.pattern: Expectations based on another country's defence, for example a public ceremony or a fixed presentation, applied to a closed viva.
difficulties.revealedBy: Preparing a long presentation for a format where none is expected, or being surprised by the length and depth of questioning.
difficulties.response: Make the local format explicit, using regulations and recent candidates' accounts.

diagnostic.task: Ask: 'What is your original contribution, and what would you do differently if you started again?'
diagnostic.strongResponse: States the contribution clearly and calibrated, identifies a genuine limitation and explains a reasoned alternative without undermining the thesis.
diagnostic.partialResponse: States the contribution but struggles to discuss limitations, or concedes too much.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Cannot state a contribution or becomes defensive.

guidance.contextNotes: Formats differ substantially: UK and Irish closed vivas with internal and external examiners and outcomes such as minor or major corrections; public defences in the Netherlands, the Nordic countries and elsewhere in continental Europe, usually held after a committee has approved the written thesis and conducted by one opponent (as in Sweden or Finland) or several committee members (as in the Netherlands); North American committee defences, preceded by proposal defences or qualifying examinations; UK outcomes that also include revise-and-resubmit or a lower award; online and hybrid vivas; and systems, including many Australian universities, that examine the thesis in writing only. Preparation should follow local regulations.

guidance.summary: Authorship is a matter of credit and accountability. The ICMJE recommendations (ICMJE 2025) define authorship by a set of criteria that all must be met, including substantial contribution, drafting or critical revision, final approval and accountability, and Brand et al. (2015) introduced the CRediT taxonomy to describe contributor roles more precisely. Conventions on author order differ across fields, and supervisors' roles in student publications vary. The Vitae RDF places research integrity and attribution within professional conduct (Vitae 2010). Teach the criteria with scenarios and practise authorship conversations.

activities.title: Authorship scenarios
learnerActions: Read five scenarios describing contributions to a paper
Decide who qualifies for authorship under ICMJE and who should be acknowledged
Write a CRediT contribution statement for one scenario
Compare decisions in groups and discuss field differences
activities.intendedInsight: Effort alone does not confer authorship; criteria include accountability and approval.
activities.rationale: Applying ICMJE (2025) and CRediT (Brand et al. 2015) to concrete cases makes abstract criteria usable.

activities.title: The authorship conversation
learnerActions: Role-play raising authorship with a supervisor or collaborator at the start of a project
Practise mitigated but clear language for proposing roles and order
Agree a written record of the discussion
activities.intendedInsight: Early, explicit conversations prevent later disputes, and they can be raised politely.
activities.rationale: Authorship disputes often arise from unspoken assumptions; the activity is a proposal grounded in professional-conduct expectations (Vitae 2010).

difficulties.pattern: The head of the lab is always an author, whatever they did.
difficulties.revealedBy: Author lists that include people with no qualifying contribution, reflecting local custom in some laboratories and fields.
difficulties.response: Discuss honorary authorship as an integrity issue using published criteria, while acknowledging the power dynamics that make it hard to challenge.

difficulties.pattern: I did all the work, so I should be first author, but I am afraid to raise it.
difficulties.revealedBy: Unresolved resentment and disputes late in projects.
difficulties.response: Practise early authorship conversations and signpost institutional guidance and support.

diagnostic.task: Ask the learner whether a person who only collected data qualifies as an author, and why.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Applies all four ICMJE criteria: notes that data acquisition can satisfy the first, so the person is acknowledged unless they are also given, and take up, the opportunity to draft or critically revise, approve the final version and accept accountability; and notes that ICMJE was written for medical journals and that other fields follow other norms.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Gives an answer based on effort or seniority, with partial reference to criteria.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Has no criteria for deciding.

guidance.contextNotes: PGT students publishing from dissertations need to understand supervisor co-authorship norms. At PGR, authorship issues arise in collaborations, publication-based theses and multi-author labs, and conventions differ markedly between, for example, biomedicine, physics, economics and the humanities.

guidance.summary: Research on multilingual scholars' publishing shows both perceived disadvantage and agency. Flowerdew (1999) surveyed and interviewed Hong Kong academics, who reported that writing in English took longer and that qualifying claims and writing introductions and discussions were particularly difficult. Lillis and Curry (2010) documented the role of literacy brokers and networks in publication and the pressures towards English-medium output, and Canagarajah (2002) identified non-discursive barriers, such as resources and access, alongside discursive ones for scholars in the periphery. Teach this topic as critical awareness that informs practical decisions, avoiding deficit framing.

activities.title: Mapping your brokers
learnerActions: List the people and services who have helped shape your texts (co-authors, supervisors, editors, translators, peers)
Classify their contributions (content, rhetoric, language)
Identify gaps and how you might fill them
Discuss the disclosure and ethics of each kind of help
activities.intendedInsight: All academic writing is mediated by networks; using brokers is normal and should be planned and acknowledged appropriately.
activities.rationale: Lillis and Curry (2010) showed how literacy brokers and networks shape publication.

activities.title: Responding to language comments
learnerActions: Analyse anonymised reviewer comments about language
Distinguish comments that identify real clarity problems from generic or biased ones
Draft professional responses to each type
activities.intendedInsight: Not all language comments are equally valid, and responses should address clarity without accepting bias.
activities.rationale: Flowerdew (1999) and Canagarajah (2002) show that language and resource issues interact with gatekeeping in English-medium publishing.

difficulties.pattern: My English is the problem; native speakers have no difficulties publishing.
difficulties.revealedBy: Attributing all rejections to language, and reluctance to submit.
difficulties.response: Acknowledge that multilingual scholars report language-related reviewer comments and real additional costs in time and money (Flowerdew 1999; Lillis & Curry 2010), and that evidence on how far language affects editorial decisions is mixed. Help the learner separate comments about clarity from comments about variety or accent, and note that writers of every background face rejection, so not every rejection is about language. Do not dismiss the learner's experience.

difficulties.pattern: Publishing in my own language does not count, so I will only write in English.
difficulties.revealedBy: Neglect of local audiences and venues where they would be valuable.
difficulties.response: Discuss multilingual dissemination strategies and their value, alongside institutional incentives.

diagnostic.task: Ask the learner what support they would seek to prepare an English-medium manuscript, and how they would acknowledge it.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Identifies appropriate brokers, distinguishes content from language help, and knows the disclosure requirements.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Identifies support but is unsure of the boundaries or disclosure.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Has no strategy, or plans to use unacknowledged help that would breach integrity rules.

guidance.contextNotes: This is a PGR topic, relevant both to learners in anglophone universities and to those in EMI and transnational contexts, where institutional pressures to publish in English may be strong.

guidance.summary: Engagement and impact are increasingly expected of researchers and are named in the Vitae RDF (Vitae 2010, sub-domain D3). Myers (1990) contrasted how the same biological research was written for specialist and popular audiences, and Hyland (2010) analysed how writers construct proximity to readers differently in popular and professional science. Teaching should focus on audience analysis, register adaptation and keeping claims calibrated when simplifying.

activities.title: One finding, three audiences
learnerActions: Choose one finding from your research
Write it for a specialist journal, a practitioner newsletter and a public blog
Compare framing, detail, register and hedging across the three
Ask a peer to check whether the claims stay accurate
activities.intendedInsight: Adapting to an audience changes framing and register, but the claim's calibration must remain accurate.
activities.rationale: Comparisons of professional and popular science writing (Myers 1990; Hyland 2010) show systematic differences in how writers relate to readers.

activities.title: Engagement plan
learnerActions: Identify an audience that could benefit from your research
Choose a channel and format suited to that audience
State the purpose and how you would know whether it worked
Present the plan for peer feedback
activities.intendedInsight: Engagement is more effective when planned around a specific audience and purpose.
activities.rationale: Vitae (2010) frames engagement and impact as a planned professional competence.

difficulties.pattern: To make it interesting, I say my study proves that coffee prevents cancer.
difficulties.revealedBy: Inflated causal or certainty claims in lay summaries.
difficulties.response: Practise plain-language hedging (may, in this study, among these participants) and test summaries on lay readers.

difficulties.pattern: Writing for the public means writing simply, so I remove all the detail.
difficulties.revealedBy: Summaries that are so general that they no longer represent the research.
difficulties.response: Distinguish simplifying language from removing substance, and keep the key finding and its basis.

diagnostic.task: Ask the learner to explain their research to you as if you were a member of the public, in one minute.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Uses accessible language, states the key finding and why it matters, and keeps claims accurate.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Is accessible but vague, or accurate but full of jargon.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Cannot adapt the explanation or misrepresents the findings.

guidance.contextNotes: PGT students may produce lay summaries or policy-facing outputs. PGR learners face funder requirements, engagement events such as three-minute thesis competitions, and online profiles.

guidance.summary: Academic self-presentation genres construct a professional identity. Ivanič (1998) frames writing as the discoursal construction of identity, and Hyland and Tse (2012) analysed article bio statements, showing how writers present credentials and affiliations and how this varies with seniority. The Vitae RDF names professional and career development as a sub-domain (Vitae 2010, B3). Teach each genre with exemplars from the target context, since CV conventions differ across countries, sectors and funders, including the growing use of narrative CVs.

activities.title: Bio comparison
learnerActions: Collect bio statements from a journal or conference in your field
Note what is included, in what order, and in which person
Compare bios of early-career and senior researchers
Write your own 100-word bio
activities.intendedInsight: Bio statements follow conventions of content and order that signal membership of a field.
activities.rationale: Hyland and Tse (2012) show that bio statements construct academic identity through selected credentials.

activities.title: Tailoring a CV
learnerActions: Extract the essential and desirable criteria from a post, studentship or fellowship advertisement
Reorder and select CV sections so that evidence for the essential criteria appears first
Rewrite entries to state your own contribution and its outcome
Peer review for consistency of format and accuracy of claims
activities.intendedInsight: A CV is an argument against criteria, not a complete record.
activities.rationale: Mapping evidence to criteria makes self-presentation explicit and checkable, and the Vitae RDF treats this as part of professional and career development (Vitae 2010). The activity is a practical proposal.

difficulties.pattern: I list everything I have ever done so the panel can see I am active.
difficulties.revealedBy: Long CVs with undifferentiated lists, minor items given the same weight as key outputs, and evidence for the post's criteria hard to find.
difficulties.response: Ask the learner to identify the three things the reader most needs to see and to make them visible on the first page. Do not insist on a fixed length; norms differ between countries and sectors.

difficulties.pattern: Including a photo, date of birth and marital status on an academic CV.
difficulties.revealedBy: CVs that follow the conventions of another national or sector context, where such details are expected.
difficulties.response: Present CV conventions as context-specific: show the target context's practice and the reasons for it, such as equality legislation, and note that the same details may be expected elsewhere. Do not treat the learner's convention as an error in general.

difficulties.pattern: My conference bio lists all my degrees and every institution I have studied at.
difficulties.revealedBy: Bios that read as short CVs, with no research focus and details irrelevant to the audience.
difficulties.response: Use bios from the same event or journal as models and ask the learner to lead with current role and research focus. Discuss when first- or third-person bios are expected.

diagnostic.task: Ask the learner to write a three-sentence bio for a conference programme.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Gives current role, research focus and a relevant achievement in the third person, concisely.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Includes relevant content but in an inappropriate person or order, or with unnecessary detail.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Writes a personal narrative or lists unrelated information.

guidance.contextNotes: In-sessional UG learners may need a short academic CV for master's applications. PGT learners prepare CVs and bios for doctoral applications and student conferences. PGR learners write academic CVs, narrative CVs for funders, bios for conferences and journals and profiles for institutional pages, and adapt them for academic and non-academic careers.
reviewNotes: Review response: R1-34 split personal statements into pub.personal-statements; this topic now covers academic CVs and biographical statements only. R5-10: the CV-convention difficulty is now coded as conceptual, not as a transfer or schooling problem.

guidance.summary: Connor and Mauranen (1999) analysed European Union research grant proposals and found that they combine research-article moves such as territory and gap with promotional moves such as benefits, importance and competence claims, which reflects the evaluative purpose of the genre. The Vitae Researcher Development Framework (Vitae 2010) treats income and funding generation as part of researcher development, so applications are also career documents. Lay summaries draw on the strategies writers use to build proximity with non-specialist readers (Hyland 2010). Teach applicants to analyse the specific call, criteria and guidance for assessors, to make the evidence for every criterion easy to find, and to calibrate promotion so that significance is clear without overclaiming.

activities.title: Criteria-to-text map
learnerActions: Copy the assessment criteria from a real call into a table
Mark where your draft addresses each criterion and quote the sentence
Add or rewrite text for any criterion without clear evidence
Ask a peer from another field to score the draft against the criteria
activities.intendedInsight: Assessors score against criteria, so the evidence for each must be easy to find.
activities.rationale: Connor and Mauranen (1999) show that grant proposals include moves, such as benefits and competence claims, that respond to evaluators; mapping makes these moves deliberate. The activity is a practitioner proposal.

activities.title: Two summaries, two readers
learnerActions: Write a 100-word technical summary of your project
Rewrite it as a lay summary for a non-specialist panel member
Check that the hedging of your claims has survived the simplification
Compare your version with lay summaries of funded projects in your area
activities.intendedInsight: A lay summary changes vocabulary, framing and detail, but not the strength of the claims.
activities.rationale: Hyland (2010) describes how writers construct proximity with readers of popular science; the activity applies this while protecting claim calibration.

difficulties.pattern: My project is important, so I explain the topic and the literature in detail and the reviewers will see its value.
difficulties.revealedBy: Applications dominated by background, with aims, plan, outputs and benefits compressed or missing.
difficulties.response: Show guidance for assessors and scoring sheets, and ask the learner to allocate words to criteria before revising. Do not strip out all background; assessors need enough context to judge significance.

difficulties.pattern: Writing about my own achievements feels like boasting, so I describe my work modestly and let the panel decide.
difficulties.revealedBy: Track-record sections that list activities without stating their significance, and heavily hedged statements of capability.
difficulties.response: Present explicit evidence of capability as a requirement of the genre rather than as arrogance, and practise sentences that link an achievement to the scheme's criteria. Comfort with self-promotion varies widely among early-career researchers of all backgrounds.

difficulties.pattern: The criteria and the expected level of detail are unclear, and successful applications are never shared.
difficulties.revealedBy: Applicants guessing at expectations and receiving very different advice from different colleagues.
difficulties.response: Teachers and research offices can collect successful applications with permission and run mock panels. Applicants should read the funder's guidance for assessors and ask research-support staff for internal review before submission.

diagnostic.task: Ask the learner to write two sentences stating the expected benefit of their research for a named group outside academia.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Names a specific beneficiary, the route by which the research could reach them and a plausible, calibrated benefit.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Names a beneficiary but states the benefit generically or with inflated certainty.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Restates the research aim or claims general importance without naming any beneficiary.

guidance.contextNotes: At PGT, the main applications are for doctoral studentships and scholarships, which often combine a proposal and a personal statement. At PGR, candidates apply for travel grants and small project grants and, near completion, for postdoctoral fellowships with full cases for support, data management plans and narrative CVs. Funder norms differ: some UK and European funders use narrative CV formats, North American agencies use their own templates, and many funders now require lay summaries and open-access commitments.

guidance.summary: Wulff, Swales and Keller (2009) analysed the discussion sessions that follow papers at a specialised conference and showed that these exchanges of questions, comments and responses have recognisable patterns, which makes them teachable. Morita (2004) showed that graduate students' participation in academic discussion is negotiated through identity and positioning, so a newcomer's silence can reflect how others position them as much as their language. The Vitae Researcher Development Framework (Vitae 2010) treats collaboration and networking as part of working with others. Teach floor questions, chairing and networking through observation of real sessions and rehearsable moves, discuss who gets access to the floor, and accept that participation takes several forms, including written questions and online chat.

activities.title: Question bank from real sessions
learnerActions: Watch recorded question-and-answer sessions from a conference in your field
Note how questioners open, connect to the talk and signal the type of question
Classify the questions as clarification, challenge, extension or comment
Prepare and practise two questions for a talk you will attend
activities.intendedInsight: Good floor questions are short, anchored in the talk and clear about what they ask.
activities.rationale: Wulff et al. (2009) show that conference discussion sessions have describable patterns; observing local recordings makes them available to newcomers. The activity is a practitioner proposal.

activities.title: Chairing and networking rehearsal
learnerActions: In groups, run a mini-session of three short talks, rotating the chair
As chair, introduce each speaker from their bio, give time signals and manage two questions
In the break, practise introducing your research in two sentences and asking about others' work
Draft a follow-up email to one person you spoke to
activities.intendedInsight: Chairing and networking use predictable moves that can be rehearsed.
activities.rationale: Morita (2004) shows that newcomers' participation depends on how they are positioned in interaction; rehearsing roles such as chair gives them legitimate ways to take the floor.

difficulties.pattern: My question has to show that I know a lot, so I give a long comment before asking.
difficulties.revealedBy: Floor questions with long preambles, several questions in one turn or no question at all.
difficulties.response: Practise a short structure: connect to the talk, ask one question, stop. Do not discourage comments altogether; in some fields extended comments are expected.

difficulties.pattern: The chair always picks senior people, and when I did speak nobody took up my point.
difficulties.revealedBy: Early-career and multilingual participants rarely given the floor or acknowledged.
difficulties.response: Discuss strategies such as signalling to the chair early, using online question tools and following up in person. Encourage organisers and chairs to allocate turns fairly, for example by taking a question from an early-career researcher first, and to accept written questions.

difficulties.pattern: Networking feels like selling myself, so I wait for people to approach me.
difficulties.revealedBy: Avoiding the social parts of conferences and not following up after events.
difficulties.response: Reframe networking as conversation about research and practise opening and closing moves. Accept quieter forms such as following up by email or on scholarly platforms, and recognise that busy events can be inaccessible or overwhelming for some participants.

diagnostic.task: Ask the learner to introduce their research to a stranger at a conference in two sentences and then ask the stranger one question about their work.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Gives a concise, accessible description of the research and asks an open question that invites conversation.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Gives an accurate but long or jargon-heavy description, or asks a closed question.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Cannot summarise the research briefly, or does not ask about the other person.

guidance.contextNotes: At PGT, students meet research seminars and departmental conferences, where observing and asking questions are the main skills. At PGR, candidates present at and later chair sessions, and networking supports careers and collaboration. Norms differ between large international conferences, small specialist workshops, practice-led events and online or hybrid formats; because cost, travel and visa barriers exclude many researchers, online participation should be treated as full participation.

guidance.summary: Bhatia (1993) analysed application letters as promotional genres in which writers present themselves in terms of the reader's selection needs, and Ivanič (1998) frames such writing as the discoursal construction of identity. Hyland and Tse (2012) showed how academics construct credibility in bio statements by selecting credentials, a related form of academic self-presentation. Teach the statement as an argument for the fit between applicant and programme, built from specific evidence, and make implicit criteria explicit. Discuss the ethics of templates, paid services and generative AI, since many institutions now ask applicants to declare or limit such help.

activities.title: Claim–evidence audit
learnerActions: Underline every claim you make about yourself in your draft
Next to each, write the specific evidence a reader would need
Delete or rewrite claims that have no evidence
Check that every criterion is addressed at least once
activities.intendedInsight: Selectors are persuaded by evidence of capability and fit, not by assertions of enthusiasm.
activities.rationale: Bhatia (1993) shows that promotional genres work by matching self-presentation to the reader's selection needs; auditing claims makes this match explicit. The activity is a practical proposal.

activities.title: Statements across contexts
learnerActions: Compare two statements from your field written for different countries or types of programme
Note differences in length, structure, research detail and personal narrative
List what your target programme's prompts ask for
Plan the sections of your statement against those prompts
activities.intendedInsight: There is no universal template; the target programme's prompts and conventions decide the shape.
activities.rationale: Treating writing as identity construction (Ivanič 1998) supports helping applicants choose how to present themselves for each context rather than imposing one model.

difficulties.pattern: I have been passionate about economics since childhood and am a hard-working person.
difficulties.revealedBy: Statements built on general traits and life narratives with no specific evidence.
difficulties.response: Ask for evidence for each claim and connect it to the criteria. Avoid imposing a single template; some programmes value personal narrative more than others.

difficulties.pattern: I found a statement online that worked for someone else, so I adapted it.
difficulties.revealedBy: Generic phrasing, details that do not fit the applicant, and wording close to published samples.
difficulties.response: Explain that reused text cannot show fit and that institutions may check statements for authenticity. Similarity or AI-detection results alone never establish misconduct; the aim is a statement that is accurately the applicant's own. Use exemplars for analysis, not as templates.

difficulties.pattern: Selection criteria are not published, and I don't know what the admissions tutor wants.
difficulties.revealedBy: Applicants writing to guessed criteria or relying on commercial advice.
difficulties.response: Help learners infer criteria from programme descriptions and scholarship guidance and encourage them to ask admissions staff. Institutions should publish what statements are assessed on, because hidden criteria disadvantage applicants without insider advice.

diagnostic.task: Ask the learner to write two sentences explaining why a named programme fits their goals.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Refers to specific features of the programme and links them to a specific aspect of the learner's experience or plans.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Gives plausible reasons that would apply to any programme in the field.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Praises the institution's reputation or ranking only.

guidance.contextNotes: In-sessional UG learners mainly need statements for master's applications, often in their final year alongside dissertation work. PGT learners apply for doctoral programmes and scholarships, where the statement accompanies a research proposal and sometimes merges with it. Conventions differ across countries, sectors and programme types; employment applications are covered by the professional applications topic, and fellowship applications by the funding applications topic.
reviewNotes: No genre analysis of statements of purpose is in the bibliography; the guidance draws on studies of related promotional and self-presentation genres. A move analysis of postgraduate statements of purpose would strengthen this topic.

guidance.summary: Tinkler and Jackson (2004) describe the UK doctoral examination process from the perspectives of candidates, examiners and supervisors, including the range of outcomes and what follows the oral, and Paltridge and Starfield (2020) discuss the examination of the thesis and examiners' expectations. Corrections are an occluded writing task: candidates rarely see other candidates' reports or corrections documents, so making the genre visible through anonymised examples is the main teaching move. Language corrections raise questions about acceptable help; Harwood, Austin and Macaulay (2009) found wide variation in what proofreaders working with students at a UK university were prepared to do, which supports checking institutional rules before using editorial support.

activities.title: From report to corrections table
learnerActions: Read an anonymised examiners' report and highlight each comment that requires action
Classify each comment as required or advisory, and as content, structure, referencing or language
Build a table with columns for the comment, the planned response, its location and its status
Agree the table with your supervisor before starting revisions
activities.intendedInsight: Corrections are manageable when they are broken down, prioritised and tracked in a document the examiner can check.
activities.rationale: Tinkler and Jackson (2004) show that outcomes and corrections processes vary and need to be understood; a tracked table makes compliance visible to the approving examiner. The activity is a practitioner proposal.

activities.title: Responses that show the change
learnerActions: Compare responses such as 'Done' with responses that quote the revised text and give page numbers
Rewrite three weak responses
Write a response explaining, politely and with reasons, how an advisory suggestion was considered but not adopted
Check that every change in the thesis appears in the table
activities.intendedInsight: A corrections document is judged on traceability: the examiner must be able to verify each change quickly.
activities.rationale: The conventions parallel those of responses to journal reviewers; the activity is a practitioner proposal based on the approving examiner's need to check each change.

difficulties.pattern: The examiners passed me with corrections, so I just need to fix the typos.
difficulties.revealedBy: Corrections tables that deal only with surface errors and leave requests for clarification or further analysis unanswered.
difficulties.response: Go through each comment with the learner to identify what is required, and point out that approval depends on substantive comments being addressed.

difficulties.pattern: The report is vague — 'strengthen the discussion' — and I don't know what the examiner wants.
difficulties.revealedBy: Minimal or uncertain revisions to vaguely worded requirements, and delays while the candidate guesses.
difficulties.response: Examiners and institutions should state required changes specifically. Learners can ask for clarification through the route the regulations allow, usually the internal examiner or the supervisor, proposing a specific interpretation for confirmation.

difficulties.pattern: After years on the thesis, rereading the examiners' criticism is very hard, so I keep putting it off.
difficulties.revealedBy: Missed internal milestones and corrections started close to the deadline.
difficulties.response: Acknowledge that this is common and plan small, scheduled tasks from the corrections table. Signpost wellbeing and disability support, and explain how to request an extension under the regulations if circumstances require it.

diagnostic.task: Give the learner one examiner comment requiring further discussion of a limitation and ask for the corrections-table entry they would write.
diagnostic.strongResponse: States the required change, describes the substantive revision and gives its location, briefly quoting the new text.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Describes a relevant change but vaguely, without a location or quoted text.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Writes 'Done' or proposes a surface edit that does not address the comment.

guidance.contextNotes: This is a PGR topic, best introduced close to submission and revisited after the examination. In the UK and Ireland, corrections follow the viva and are approved by one or more examiners within set deadlines. In many continental European systems, the committee requests changes before approving the thesis for public defence. In Australia and other systems with written-only examination, candidates respond to several written reports without an oral. Revise-and-resubmit outcomes involve substantial new writing and sometimes a second oral examination.

guidance.summary: Thomson and Kamler (2013) treat writing for peer-reviewed journals as identifying a contribution for a particular journal's readers and joining their conversation, which is a different rhetorical task from demonstrating competence to thesis examiners. W. L. Belcher (2019) gives practical routes for revising existing work, including thesis chapters, into articles. Bretag and Mahmud (2009) discuss when reusing one's own text is appropriate and when it becomes self-plagiarism, which bears on reuse in both directions. Teach the move from thesis to article as re-scoping and reframing rather than cutting, and make journal and institutional reuse policies part of the task.

activities.title: One paper, one argument
learnerActions: List the claims your thesis makes
Choose one claim that could stand alone and find a journal whose recent articles discuss it
Draft a 150-word abstract for that article
List what the article needs from the thesis and what it does not
activities.intendedInsight: An article is built around one argument for one readership; the thesis is a source, not a template.
activities.rationale: Thomson and Kamler (2013) frame article writing around a contribution to a specific journal's conversation; the activity applies this to thesis material.

activities.title: Reuse decisions
learnerActions: Read your target journal's and institution's policies on prior publication of theses and on text reuse
Mark passages of your draft article that reproduce thesis or earlier article text
Decide for each passage whether to rewrite, cite or disclose
Draft the disclosure sentence for your cover letter or acknowledgements
activities.intendedInsight: Reuse is governed by policies that differ between journals and institutions, and transparency is needed in both directions.
activities.rationale: Bretag and Mahmud (2009) show that the line between appropriate textual reuse and self-plagiarism depends on context and disclosure.

difficulties.pattern: I will cut my chapter to 8,000 words and send it to a journal.
difficulties.revealedBy: Submissions that read as shortened chapters, with thesis signposting, an extended literature review and a contribution addressed to examiners.
difficulties.response: Ask the learner to write the article's contribution statement for the journal's readers first and then select from the chapter. Do not imply that thesis chapters are unpublishable; many can be published after reframing.

difficulties.pattern: It's my own work, so I can reuse my thesis text in my articles, and my articles in my thesis, without saying so.
difficulties.revealedBy: Undisclosed overlap with the thesis or with earlier publications, flagged at submission or examination.
difficulties.response: Explain disclosure conventions and publishers' reuse policies and practise disclosure sentences. Similarity reports show overlap but do not decide whether reuse is acceptable; policies and disclosure do.

difficulties.pattern: My supervisor expects to be an author on every paper from my thesis, but we have never discussed it.
difficulties.revealedBy: Uncertainty or conflict about authorship late in the writing process.
difficulties.response: Encourage an early, documented authorship conversation based on published criteria and the institution's authorship policy. Supervisors and departments should make their authorship practices explicit, since norms differ by field.

diagnostic.task: Ask the learner to state, in one sentence each, the contribution of one thesis chapter as written for examiners and as it would be written for a named journal.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Produces two clearly different framings, the journal version addressing the journal's readership and conversation.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Produces two statements that differ mainly in length.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Cannot identify a stand-alone contribution in the chapter.

guidance.contextNotes: This is a PGR topic, often taught in the final year and after submission; it can also help PGT graduates publishing from dissertations with their supervisors. In theses by publication the direction is reversed, since published papers are reproduced in the thesis, so reuse permissions and contribution statements matter more. Whether a thesis counts as prior publication varies between fields, journals and countries.

guidance.summary: Open research practices create new required texts in submissions, theses and grant applications. The FAIR principles (Wilkinson et al. 2016) describe what makes research data findable, accessible, interoperable and reusable and underpin many data management plan templates. The European Code of Conduct for Research Integrity (ALLEA 2023) treats open and transparent practice, including appropriate data management and sharing, as part of good research practice, and the ICMJE recommendations (ICMJE 2025) require data-sharing statements for clinical trials. EAP teaching concentrates on the precision and consistency of these statements and on explaining legitimate restrictions, rather than treating openness as all or nothing, since qualitative, sensitive and commercially restricted data raise different questions.

activities.title: Statement audit
learnerActions: Collect data availability statements from recent articles in your target journals
Rank them from vague (available on request) to specific (repository, identifier, licence and conditions)
Note how restrictions are explained
