Write the statement for your own study
activities.intendedInsight: Availability statements vary greatly in precision; specific statements can be checked and vague ones cannot.
activities.rationale: The FAIR principles (Wilkinson et al. 2016) define properties such as findability and accessibility that a specific statement can demonstrate; the activity is a practitioner proposal.

activities.title: Plan, consent and report alignment
learnerActions: Lay out your data management plan, participant consent wording and draft availability statement side by side
Mark any contradictions, such as plans to share data that participants were told would be destroyed
Revise the documents so that they agree
Draft a sentence reporting any deviation from your preregistration or plan
activities.intendedInsight: Open-research texts are commitments that must agree with ethics documents and with what was actually done.
activities.rationale: Research-integrity codes (ALLEA 2023) treat transparent and consistent handling of data as part of good research practice.

difficulties.pattern: Open research means I must put all my data online.
difficulties.revealedBy: Plans to share identifiable or confidential data, or refusal to engage with sharing at all because the data are sensitive.
difficulties.response: Teach the principle that data should be as open as possible and as closed as necessary, and the range of options such as controlled access, anonymised subsets, metadata-only records and justified restrictions. Use qualitative as well as quantitative exemplars.

difficulties.pattern: Data available on request from the corresponding author.
difficulties.revealedBy: Availability statements copied from older articles, which many funders and journals no longer accept on their own.
difficulties.response: Show the target journal's and funder's current requirements and practise specific statements. Do not suggest that request-based access is always wrong; it can be appropriate when justified and properly managed.

difficulties.pattern: My funder, university and journal give different rules on licences and open access, and they keep changing.
difficulties.revealedBy: Confusion about which licence or version to deposit, and missed deposit requirements.
difficulties.response: Show learners where current policies are published and who in the library or research office advises on them, and teach the questions to ask rather than rules that may soon be outdated. Institutions should provide single, current guidance.

diagnostic.task: Ask the learner what they would write in a data availability statement for their current project, and why.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Specifies the data, location, access conditions and licence, and justifies any restriction with reference to consent or legal requirements.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Identifies what can be shared but is vague about location, conditions or reasons for restriction.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Writes 'available on request', or says that data sharing does not apply, without considering options.

guidance.contextNotes: At PGT, open-research texts appear mainly in psychology and health dissertations that require preregistration or data deposit. At PGR, candidates write data management plans, availability statements and, increasingly, preprints and registered reports, and must meet funder open-access and rights-retention policies. Practices vary by field: preregistration is common in parts of psychology and clinical research, preprints in physics, computing and biology, and qualitative and humanities researchers often adapt openness to protect participants and interpretive work.
reviewNotes: Review response: R6-02 also lists ORCID and persistent identifiers; these are named in the description but not assessed separately, because registering an identifier involves little language work.

guidance.summary: Teach IMRaD as a conventional answer to a reader's questions (why, how, what was found, what it means) and as a hypothesis to test against the learner's own disciplinary exemplars, not as a template. Move studies show both a stable core and real variation: Kanoksilapatham (2005) describes a predictable move structure across sections of biochemistry articles, whereas Yang and Allison (2003) show that in applied linguistics the functions of results, discussion and conclusion overlap across section boundaries. Rhetorical consciousness-raising with discipline-specific exemplars (Swales 1990; Cheng 2018) lets mixed-discipline groups compare findings productively.

activities.title: Headings-stripped sorting
learnerActions: Take an article from your own field with headings and section breaks removed
Mark where you think each section begins and write a one-line function label for it
Compare your segmentation with the original and with a partner from a different discipline
Record one convention of your field that differs from canonical IMRaD and suggest why
activities.intendedInsight: Section boundaries are signalled by rhetorical function and by language such as tense, citation density and hedging, and the conventional order varies by field.
activities.rationale: Genre-based consciousness-raising asks learners to notice function–form relations in authentic exemplars; cross-disciplinary comparison guards against generalising one model (Swales 1990; Cheng 2018).

activities.title: Reader-question mapping
learnerActions: List the questions a reader in your field brings to a research article
Map each question to the section that answers it in two field-specific articles
Identify any question answered in an unexpected place, for example limitations in Methods
Discuss why that placement might suit the field or the journal
activities.intendedInsight: Macrostructure is a contract with the reader; variants arise when fields ask different questions or build knowledge differently.
activities.rationale: A functional framing supports transfer to non-IMRaD genres and discourages template-driven writing; Yang and Allison (2003) document functions spreading across section boundaries.

difficulties.pattern: Every research paper must have these four sections, so my history or design project is wrong if it doesn't.
difficulties.revealedBy: Learners in humanities, theoretical or practice-based fields force IMRaD headings onto argument-led work, or describe published papers from their field as badly structured.
difficulties.response: Show exemplars from the learner's field and ask what organising principle they use (argument, chronology, case, theme). Present IMRaD as one family of structures tied to empirical reporting, not as the academic norm.

difficulties.pattern: Interpretation and comparison with the literature are placed in Results, leaving the Discussion to restate findings.
difficulties.revealedBy: Drafts with heavily evaluative results and short, repetitive discussions containing few explanations or comparisons with prior work.
difficulties.response: Have learners colour-code a draft by function (report, comment, interpret, compare) and check the distribution against field exemplars. Do not impose a ban on commentary in Results, because the acceptable level of commentary varies by field; the aim is a fit with field norms.

diagnostic.task: Ask the learner to bring one recent article from their target journal or field and explain, in three minutes, where its argument is made and why it is organised as it is.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Identifies the structure accurately, names at least one field-specific variant and explains it in terms of what the field counts as evidence or how readers use the article.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Names the sections correctly but treats variation as error, or cannot say why the field departs from IMRaD.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Cannot identify section functions or assumes all academic texts follow essay structure.

guidance.contextNotes: On postgraduate pre-sessionals IMRaD is mainly a reading tool for navigating articles before an extended project. At UG and PGT it becomes a writing frame for project reports and dissertations, where departmental handbooks may impose headings. At PGR the emphasis shifts to variants such as article-based theses, theory chapters and merged results and discussion, and to the writer's informed choices within field norms.

guidance.summary: Treat research questions as the hinge between the gap and the design: they should follow from the literature and determine what data and analysis are needed. Creswell and Creswell (2018) offer scripts for purpose statements, questions and hypotheses across qualitative, quantitative and mixed designs, and Bunton (2002) shows that statements of purpose and questions are a recurrent element of PhD thesis introductions. A practitioner proposal, not a tested one, is to revise the learner's own questions repeatedly against their methods rather than to rely on generic question-writing exercises.

activities.title: Alignment table
learnerActions: Write your aim and each research question in the first column of a table
In further columns, record for each question the data source, the analysis and the kind of answer it will produce
Mark any question whose row cannot be completed, or whose answer is yes or no
Revise or remove those questions and explain the changes to a peer
activities.intendedInsight: A research question is only as good as its fit with the data and analysis that will answer it.
activities.rationale: Making alignment explicit turns an abstract quality criterion into a checkable procedure and mirrors how examiners read across chapters (Paltridge & Starfield 2020).

activities.title: Question form by design
learnerActions: Sort a set of published research questions and hypotheses into exploratory, descriptive, explanatory and confirmatory types
Note the grammatical forms each type uses (wh-questions, 'to what extent', directional hypotheses)
Rewrite one of your questions in the form suited to your design
activities.intendedInsight: Question form signals the design and the type of claim the study will be able to make.
activities.rationale: Creswell and Creswell (2018) link the wording of purpose statements and questions to the design tradition, which gives learners a principled basis for choosing a form.

difficulties.pattern: My question is 'What is the impact of social media on students?' which covers everything I am interested in.
difficulties.revealedBy: Questions that name a broad topic with no population, context, construct or type of answer, and methods that could not possibly answer them.
difficulties.response: Ask the learner to say what a satisfying answer would look like and what data would produce it, then narrow the question until it can be answered. Avoid supplying a rewritten question, since ownership of the question matters at PGT and PGR level.

difficulties.pattern: Questions drift: the introduction asks one thing, the methods measure another and the discussion answers a third.
difficulties.revealedBy: Inconsistent wording of aims across chapters, or findings reported for questions never posed.
difficulties.response: Have the learner paste the exact wording of each question into the opening of the methods, results and discussion and reconcile any differences. Do not treat this as a language error; it is usually the result of the project evolving, so the fix is to update the questions or to signal the change.

diagnostic.task: Ask the learner to read out their research questions and say, for each, what data will answer it and what form the answer will take.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Each question is scoped and answerable, its data and analysis are named without hesitation, and hypothesis language, if used, matches the design.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Questions are answerable but at least one is too broad, is a yes/no question or is only loosely linked to the data.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Questions restate the topic, or the learner cannot link them to any data or analysis.

guidance.contextNotes: Postgraduate pre-sessional projects need modest, answerable questions within weeks. UG and PGT dissertations often require supervisor approval of questions early, so formulation and alignment checks are most useful at proposal stage. At PGR, questions are expected to evolve, and the focus moves to tracking and justifying that evolution, including in progression reviews.

guidance.summary: The niche is the pivot of a research introduction. Swales (1990) described niche-establishing options as counter-claiming, indicating a gap, question-raising and continuing a tradition, and Swales (2004) revised Move 2 to centre on indicating a gap or adding to what is known, with an optional positive justification. Samraj (2002) shows disciplinary variation in how and where niches are established, and Kwan (2006) found niche-creating moves recurring through the bodies of doctoral literature reviews. Teach learners to analyse niche language in field exemplars and to ground every gap claim in cited work, with calibrated scope.

activities.title: Niche-type hunt
learnerActions: Collect the niche sentences from eight introductions in your field
Classify each as counter-claim, gap, question, continuation or extension
Underline the signalling resources (contrastive connectors, negative quantifiers, evaluative adjectives, present perfect)
Compare frequencies with a partner from a different discipline
activities.intendedInsight: Fields favour different niche types; a gentle 'extension' niche may be more persuasive in some fields than a direct counter-claim.
activities.rationale: Swales' (1990, 2004) move model and Samraj's (2002) disciplinary findings give learners categories to test against their own field's texts.

activities.title: Stress-testing the gap
learnerActions: Write your niche statement
Swap with a peer, who tries to find one study that falsifies it
Narrow or rephrase the statement so that it survives, for example by naming population, setting, method or time-scale
Check that the revised gap still leads to your aims
activities.intendedInsight: A precise, bounded gap is more defensible and more persuasive than a sweeping one.
activities.rationale: Reviewers and examiners routinely challenge overstated gap claims; peer challenge rehearses this and links niche construction to claim calibration.

difficulties.pattern: No research has ever been done on this topic.
difficulties.revealedBy: Absolute gap claims with no supporting citations, often contradicted by sources the learner has already cited.
difficulties.response: Ask the learner to evidence the gap with the closest existing studies and to state precisely what those studies do not do. Do not simply replace 'no' with 'little'; the problem is the unsupported scope of the claim, not its wording.

difficulties.pattern: My gap is that this has not been studied in my country, so the study is justified.
difficulties.revealedBy: Niches that rest only on a new location, population or period, with no argument for why the difference matters.
difficulties.response: Ask the learner to explain what might be different in the new context and why that matters for theory or practice, and show niches that justify a contextual extension. Do not dismiss contextual gaps; they are legitimate when their significance is argued.

diagnostic.task: Give the learner a four-study review paragraph and a one-sentence aim; ask them to write the two sentences that connect them.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Writes a niche that is traceable to the cited studies, bounded in scope, uses evaluative and contrastive resources and leads directly to the aim.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Signals a gap with appropriate language but the gap is generic, or does not connect clearly to the aim.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Omits the niche, makes an unsupported absolute claim or restates the aim.

guidance.contextNotes: Postgraduate pre-sessional and UG learners usually meet gap language through short introductions to projects. At PGT the gap justifies the dissertation and is often examined explicitly in marking criteria. At PGR, niches must survive expert scrutiny, recur across chapters and connect to a claimed contribution.

guidance.summary: Use the Create-a-Research-Space model (Swales 1990, revised in Swales 2004) as an analytical lens and planning tool for introductions, while making disciplinary variation explicit. Samraj (2002) found background material and recursive move cycles in some fields that the original model did not anticipate, and Bunton (2002) describes additional steps in PhD thesis introductions, such as outlining the thesis structure and defining terms. Genre analysis of the learner's own exemplars, followed by drafting and move-annotated peer review, is the core sequence.

activities.title: Move-annotate and reconstruct
learnerActions: Annotate an introduction from your field sentence by sentence for moves and steps
Note where moves recur in cycles and where optional steps such as summarising findings appear
Reconstruct a jumbled introduction from a different field and compare its structure with yours
Write a move outline for your own introduction before drafting
activities.intendedInsight: The CARS moves are a recognisable logic that fields realise differently, and outlining by move separates rhetorical planning from sentence-level drafting.
activities.rationale: Move analysis of authentic exemplars is the established genre-based method for research writing (Swales 1990, 2004), and cross-field comparison exposes variation such as that reported by Samraj (2002).

activities.title: Article versus thesis introduction
learnerActions: Compare an article introduction and a PhD or master's thesis introduction from your field
List the steps the thesis introduction adds (for example scope, definitions, chapter outline)
Decide which of these your own text needs and draft them
activities.intendedInsight: Thesis introductions carry additional reader-orientation work because of their length and their examiner audience.
activities.rationale: Bunton (2002) shows that PhD introductions extend the CARS moves with thesis-orientation steps.

difficulties.pattern: I start with the history of the topic from ancient times and get to my study on page five.
difficulties.revealedBy: Long, unfocused Move 1 with generic centrality claims ('since the dawn of time', 'in today's world') and a late or missing niche, often modelled on the broad-to-narrow introductions taught for school and test essays.
difficulties.response: Have the learner count sentences per move and compare with exemplars, then compress Move 1 to what the niche needs. Avoid banning background outright, since some fields use substantial background.

difficulties.pattern: The CARS model is a formula, so every introduction should have exactly these three moves in order.
difficulties.revealedBy: Mechanical introductions with one sentence per step and phrasebank formulae, regardless of field.
difficulties.response: Return to field exemplars showing cycling and optional steps, and ask the learner to justify each choice by what readers in their field expect.

difficulties.pattern: Move 3 announces the topic but not the questions, so readers cannot see what the study will answer.
difficulties.revealedBy: Announcements such as 'This study will look at…' with no aims, questions or hypotheses.
difficulties.response: Ask the learner to insert their research questions verbatim into Move 3 and check that they answer the niche.

diagnostic.task: Ask the learner to annotate their own draft introduction by move in the margin and to explain one optional step they included or omitted.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Annotation is accurate, the niche follows from the reviewed work, Move 3 answers the niche and optional steps are justified by field convention.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Moves are present, but Move 1 is overlong or generic, or the link between niche and announcement is weak.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Cannot identify moves in their own text, or the introduction lacks a niche or an announcement of the study.

guidance.contextNotes: On postgraduate pre-sessionals the focus is a short, complete CARS introduction for the extended project. UG and PGT learners apply it to dissertation introductions, often with departmental templates. PGR learners need thesis-level introductions and article introductions written for different readers, and attention to disciplinary variation.

guidance.summary: Teach the research literature review as an argument about the state of knowledge that makes room for the writer's study. Kwan (2006) found an introduction–body–conclusion structure in applied linguistics doctoral reviews, with the body cycling through moves that establish territory and create niches, although writers did not always relate the literature to their own research. Feak and Swales (2009) frame the review as a 'research story' with deliberate choices of citation form, metadiscourse and stance. Petrić (2007) found that higher-rated master's theses used citation for a wider range of functions, notably application and comparison, which can be made explicit in teaching. Kamler and Thomson (2014) also treat the review as identity work: writers must position themselves with authority among established scholars.

activities.title: Paragraph function audit
learnerActions: Number the paragraphs of your draft review
Write beside each one the claim it makes and how it serves your study (justifies a question, a concept or a design choice)
Highlight sentences that only report a source and those that evaluate, compare or apply it
Revise two report-only paragraphs so that they make a positioning claim
activities.intendedInsight: Every paragraph of a research review should do positioning work, and evaluation and application of sources are what make the writer's voice visible.
activities.rationale: Petrić's (2007) finding on citation functions in higher- and lower-rated theses, and Kwan's (2006) observation that writers do not always connect literature to their own study, suggest these are the points to make explicit.

activities.title: From matrix to story
learnerActions: Build a synthesis matrix of your key sources by theme, finding and method
Identify two or three tensions or trends across the matrix
Sequence these as a 'research story' leading to your niche
Draft topic sentences that state the story's claims before adding the sources
activities.intendedInsight: Organisation should come from the argument about the field, not from the order in which sources were read.
activities.rationale: Feak and Swales (2009) treat the review as a narrative with a purpose; planning claims before sources counters source-by-source organisation.

difficulties.pattern: Smith (2015) found…; Jones (2017) found…; Lee (2019) found… — one paragraph per source.
difficulties.revealedBy: Integral citations opening most sentences, a list-like structure and little evaluative language.
difficulties.response: Have the learner rewrite one paragraph with a topic sentence that makes a claim about the group of studies and uses non-integral citation for support. Do not simply ban integral citation, which is valuable for foregrounding key scholars and contrasting positions.

difficulties.pattern: I must include everything ever written on my topic to show the examiner I have read widely.
difficulties.revealedBy: Very long reviews covering loosely related literature, with no criteria for inclusion and no links to the study.
difficulties.response: Ask the learner to justify each section by reference to a research question or a design decision, and to cut or condense what cannot be justified.

difficulties.pattern: I am only a student, so I cannot judge published work.
difficulties.revealedBy: Reviews in which every study is presented neutrally or approvingly and no tensions or weaknesses are named.
difficulties.response: Present evaluation as a disciplinary expectation that novice writers of all backgrounds find difficult, model mitigated evaluation from published reviews and discuss authorial identity explicitly (Kamler & Thomson 2014). Show how a niche can be built from tensions between studies, which makes evaluation a structural need rather than a personal judgement.

diagnostic.task: Ask the learner to give a two-minute oral summary of their literature review without notes, then to say how it leads to their research questions.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Summarises the review as a small number of claims about the field, with tensions and a gap, and links these explicitly to the questions.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Summarises themes accurately but cannot say how they justify the study, or lists authors rather than claims.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Recounts sources one by one with no organising claim or link to the study.

guidance.contextNotes: At PGT, the review is typically a dissertation chapter, marked for criticality and relevance to the study. At PGR, the review may be distributed across chapters or articles, must demonstrate command of the field and is revisited throughout the project, including updating before submission. Undergraduate dissertations and coursework reviews use the student literature review genre instead.

guidance.summary: Frameworks are a common source of difficulty because their form and even their existence vary by field: social science and education theses typically expect an explicit framework, whereas many experimental papers embed theory in the introduction. Creswell and Creswell (2018) distinguish how theory is used deductively in quantitative work and more variably in qualitative and mixed designs, which helps learners decide where and how the framework should appear. Teaching should centre on tracing concepts forward into methods and analysis, so that the framework does visible work, and on discussing field exemplars, including the variation that Paltridge and Starfield (2020) note in how theses handle theory.

activities.title: Concept tracing
learnerActions: List the three to five key concepts of your framework
For each, find where it appears in your methods (instrument, coding frame, variable) and in your findings
Mark concepts that never reappear after the framework chapter
Either connect them to the analysis or remove them, and revise the framework section accordingly
activities.intendedInsight: A framework is justified by what it does in the analysis; concepts that do no work weaken the thesis.
activities.rationale: Creswell and Creswell (2018) present theory as something that shapes questions, data and interpretation; tracing makes this relationship checkable.

activities.title: Framework exemplar comparison
learnerActions: Read framework sections from two theses in your field
Identify how each defines constructs, justifies its theory choice and anticipates the analysis
Note what the writers say about alternatives they did not adopt
Draft a justification paragraph for your own framework that names one alternative
activities.intendedInsight: Justifying a framework involves showing that alternatives were considered, not only that the chosen theory is well known.
activities.rationale: Analysing successful theses is a core strategy recommended for thesis writers by Paltridge and Starfield (2020).

difficulties.pattern: My framework chapter summarises Bourdieu's theory in detail, but I don't refer to it again.
difficulties.revealedBy: Framework chapters that read as textbook summaries, and findings chapters with no theoretical vocabulary.
difficulties.response: Use concept tracing and ask the learner to rewrite the chapter around the concepts they actually apply. Avoid requiring more theory; the issue is application, not coverage.

difficulties.pattern: Theoretical framework, conceptual framework and literature review are the same thing.
difficulties.revealedBy: Learners are unsure what to include, duplicate content across chapters or follow supervisors' conflicting terminology.
difficulties.response: Acknowledge that the terms are used inconsistently across fields and supervisors. Help the learner agree working definitions with their supervisor and check them against departmental theses.

diagnostic.task: Ask the learner why they chose their framework rather than one named alternative, and where its concepts appear in their analysis.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Gives a reasoned justification tied to the research questions, names the alternative's limitations for this study and points to specific analytic uses.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Justifies the choice in general terms (it is widely used, my supervisor suggested it) or can point to only one analytic use.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Cannot explain the choice or link the framework to the analysis.

guidance.contextNotes: At PGT, frameworks are expected mainly in social science, education and business dissertations, and may be brief. At PGR the framework is often a chapter or a major section that examiners scrutinise closely and that may be revised late as the analysis matures. Learners in experimental sciences may need only to recognise the concept.
reviewNotes: Disciplinary practice on whether a separate framework section is expected varies widely; check with departmental exemplars before teaching it as a requirement.

guidance.summary: Methods sections are more rhetorical than they look: Cotos, Huffman and Link (2017) describe moves for contextualising the study's methods, describing the study and establishing credibility, and Lim (2006) showed management writers justifying sampling and procedures, not only describing them. Kanoksilapatham (2005) found the methods moves of biochemistry articles centred on describing materials and procedures, so the degree of justification varies by field. Teach learners to analyse exemplars from their own journals or departments and to check completeness against reporting guidelines, while treating voice and tense as field choices rather than fixed rules.

activities.title: Describe versus justify
learnerActions: Highlight descriptive statements in one colour and justifying statements in another in two field exemplars
Note which decisions are justified and how (rationale, precedent citation, reference to the research questions)
Apply the same highlighting to your own draft
Add justification for the two decisions a sceptical reader would question most
activities.intendedInsight: Credibility comes from justified choices; a methods section that only describes leaves readers to doubt the design.
activities.rationale: The credibility-establishing move identified by Cotos et al. (2017) and the justification steps in Lim (2006) give learners named targets for revision.

activities.title: Replication check
learnerActions: Exchange methods drafts with a peer in a related field
Try to write a step-by-step protocol from the peer's text
Note every point where you had to guess
Return the list and revise your own draft
activities.intendedInsight: Experts underestimate the detail readers need, and gaps become visible only when someone tries to follow the procedure.
activities.rationale: Peer reconstruction makes the reader's needs concrete; the activity is a proposal adapted from replication logic, not a tested intervention.

difficulties.pattern: The passive is more objective, so I must never write 'we' or 'I' in methods.
difficulties.revealedBy: Strained agentless passives, dangling modifiers ('After collecting the data, it was analysed') or inconsistency with the learner's target journal.
difficulties.response: Show the variation in voice in the learner's target journals and discuss when an agent matters. Present voice as a field and journal choice, not a rule about objectivity.

difficulties.pattern: Methods are just a list of what I did, in the order I did it.
difficulties.revealedBy: Chronological narratives including irrelevant steps, missing analysis procedures and no justification.
difficulties.response: Return to the function of methods within the macrostructure and reorganise by conventional sub-sections. Ask what the reader needs in order to trust and evaluate the findings.

diagnostic.task: Ask the learner to identify the riskiest decision in their design and show where their methods section justifies it.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Names a consequential decision, points to a justification using rationale or precedent, and notes any limitation it creates.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Identifies a decision but the text describes it without justification, or justifies a trivial decision only.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Cannot identify a design decision that needs justification, or the methods section is purely narrative.

guidance.contextNotes: UG project reports often follow departmental templates and lab-report conventions. PGT dissertations in the social sciences may require a separate methodology chapter with paradigm discussion, which overlaps with methods writing. PGR learners writing articles must compress methods to journal norms and use supplementary materials, while thesis methods chapters are often extensive.
reviewNotes: dss.methodology-justification now depends on this topic: this topic covers the description and local justification of procedures in a methods section, and the DSS topic covers paradigm-level methodology chapters.

guidance.summary: Results writing extends data commentary to a whole section organised around research questions. Yang and Allison (2003) found results sections in applied linguistics that included comment on results as well as reporting, and Basturkmen (2009) found that published research articles developed commentary more extensively than master's dissertations did. Swales and Feak (2012) provide accessible practice in location, highlighting and comment. Teach the field's tolerance for commentary explicitly, using exemplars, and pair it with selectivity: what to say in prose and what to leave in visuals.

activities.title: Select, don't recite
learnerActions: Take a table from your own data and list every pattern it shows
Rank the patterns by relevance to your research questions
Write a results paragraph using only the top two or three patterns
Compare it with an earlier draft that reported every value
activities.intendedInsight: Results prose selects and interprets for the reader; repeating the table adds length without adding meaning.
activities.rationale: Location–highlighting–comment sequences in data commentary (Swales & Feak 2012) give a structure for selection.

activities.title: How much comment here?
learnerActions: Mark the comment statements (explanation, comparison, evaluation) in three results sections from your field
Estimate the proportion of comment to report in each
Decide what level of commentary your own results section should include and check it with your supervisor
activities.intendedInsight: The boundary between Results and Discussion is a field convention that writers can observe and match.
activities.rationale: Yang and Allison (2003) and Basturkmen (2009) show that commentary in results varies across writers and genres, so learners need to calibrate to their own field.

difficulties.pattern: Every number in the table is important, so I describe them all.
difficulties.revealedBy: Paragraphs listing values in table order, with no highlighting or link to the research questions.
difficulties.response: Ask the learner what the reader should remember from the table and build the paragraph around that. Do not simply impose a word limit; teach selection criteria.

difficulties.pattern: Findings are stated as facts about the world ('Students prefer online learning') rather than as findings of this study.
difficulties.revealedBy: Present-tense generalisations in results without reference to the sample or data, and unhedged comments.
difficulties.response: Contrast 'participants in this study reported…' with general claims, and practise tense and hedging choices that keep the scope of results claims explicit.

diagnostic.task: Give a two-variable table and one research question; ask for a short results paragraph in ten minutes.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Locates the table, highlights the patterns relevant to the question, uses tense consistently and adds proportionate comment.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Reports accurately but lists too many values or omits the link to the question.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Repeats the table in prose, misreads values or presents results as general truths.

guidance.contextNotes: UG lab and project reports often require strict separation of results and discussion. PGT dissertations vary, and qualitative dissertations frequently merge findings and discussion. PGR writers must match target-journal conventions and handle multiple results chapters in a thesis.

guidance.summary: Statistical reporting combines formatting conventions, which can be taught through style guides such as the APA Publication Manual (APA 2020), with interpretive language that demands statistical literacy (Gal 2002). The ASA statement on p-values (Wasserstein & Lazar 2016) gives an authoritative basis for teaching learners not to equate p < .05 with importance or truth and to report effect sizes and uncertainty. EAP teachers need not teach statistics, but they can require every statistic to be accompanied by an accurate plain-language interpretation and can target the formulaic misstatements that reviewers flag.

activities.title: Output to prose
learnerActions: Take software output for one test from your own analysis
Write the reporting sentence in your target style, checking symbols, italics, decimals and exact p-values against the style guide
Add a sentence saying what the result means for your research question, including the size of the effect
Swap with a peer who checks the format and challenges the interpretation
activities.intendedInsight: A statistic in the text needs both conventional form and an interpretation that a reader can evaluate.
activities.rationale: Style-guide formats (APA 2020) are learnable rules; pairing them with interpretation addresses the literacy gap described by Gal (2002).

activities.title: Misstatement clinic
learnerActions: Read a set of reporting sentences containing common errors (proof language, 'trend towards significance', non-significance as no difference)
Identify the error in each and explain why it misleads
Rewrite each sentence accurately
activities.intendedInsight: Some familiar phrases in published papers misrepresent what p-values show.
activities.rationale: The ASA statement (Wasserstein & Lazar 2016) sets out principles for p-value interpretation that can be applied directly to sentence revision.

difficulties.pattern: The result was significant, so the intervention clearly works.
difficulties.revealedBy: Boosted claims attached to p-values, no effect sizes, and 'significant' used in both its statistical and everyday senses.
difficulties.response: Separate statistical significance, effect size and practical importance in the learner's sentences, and reserve 'significant' for its statistical sense in results. Refer statistical misunderstandings to supervisors or statistics support rather than correcting the analysis yourself.

difficulties.pattern: Inconsistent formatting: p = 0.000, mixed decimal places, values duplicated in tables and text.
difficulties.revealedBy: Surface inconsistencies that reviewers and examiners notice quickly.
difficulties.response: Provide a style-guide checklist and ask learners to run it as a separate editing pass. Do not spend class time on rules the checklist covers; reserve discussion for interpretation.

diagnostic.task: Give the output of a non-significant comparison with a moderate effect size and a wide confidence interval; ask for a two-sentence report and interpretation.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Reports in correct format with effect size and interval, and interprets the result as inconclusive rather than as evidence of no difference.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Formats correctly but omits the effect size, or interprets non-significance as 'no difference'.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Misformats the statistic and misinterprets it, for example as proof or as 'nearly significant'.

guidance.contextNotes: UG reports usually require basic descriptive and inferential reporting. PGT dissertations in the social and health sciences often involve the first independent statistical reporting. PGR writers face journal-specific requirements and reporting guidelines and often reviewer demands for effect sizes and confidence intervals.

guidance.summary: Qualitative findings are persuasive when themes are presented as analytic claims that extracts illustrate and evidence, not as collections of quotations. Braun and Clarke (2006) caution that themes should be analytic constructions rather than summaries of what participants said, and that extracts need analytic narrative around them; their later account of reflexive thematic analysis (Braun & Clarke 2019) stresses that themes are generated by the researcher rather than 'emerging', and that coding-agreement statistics do not fit reflexive designs, points that examiners and reviewers now often raise. The APA's qualitative reporting standards (APA 2020) and Creswell and Creswell (2018) describe expectations about transparency, reflexivity and evidence. EAP teaching can focus on the language of the claim–extract–commentary unit and on keeping analyst and participant voices distinct.

activities.title: Claim–extract–comment frames
learnerActions: Identify the claim, extract and commentary in three findings paragraphs from published qualitative studies in your field
Note the language used to introduce extracts and to return to the analyst's voice
Rewrite one of your own quotation-heavy paragraphs into claim–extract–comment units
activities.intendedInsight: Extracts serve the analytic claim; the commentary after an extract is where interpretation happens.
activities.rationale: Braun and Clarke (2006) emphasise analytic narrative around extracts; making the unit explicit gives learners a revisable structure.

activities.title: Prevalence without pseudo-counting
learnerActions: Collect expressions used in your field's qualitative papers to indicate how widespread a pattern is (most, several, two participants, only one)
Discuss when numbers help and when they mislead
Revise your own findings to signal prevalence and divergence consistently
activities.intendedInsight: Readers need to know how typical a pattern is, but counts should be used in ways consistent with the methodology.
activities.rationale: Transparency about the basis of claims is a common expectation in qualitative reporting standards (APA 2020); the specific practice of signalling prevalence varies by tradition.

difficulties.pattern: The quotations speak for themselves.
difficulties.revealedBy: Paragraphs consisting of a theme label followed by several long extracts with little or no commentary.
difficulties.response: Ask the learner to write what each extract shows before including it, and to cut extracts that do not support a stated claim. Avoid simply asking for fewer quotations without teaching the claim–commentary structure.

difficulties.pattern: It is unclear whether a statement is the participant's view or the researcher's interpretation.
difficulties.revealedBy: Unattributed paraphrases of participants presented as findings, and reporting verbs that blur the two voices.
difficulties.response: Practise attribution (participants described…, as Ana put it…) and averral (this suggests…) and have learners colour-code voices in a draft.

difficulties.pattern: Three themes emerged from the data, and two coders agreed on most codes.
difficulties.revealedBy: Analysis accounts in which themes appear to form by themselves, or that combine reflexive thematic analysis with inter-rater agreement figures without justification.
difficulties.response: Discuss how the chosen version of thematic analysis positions the researcher, and ask learners to describe their analytic decisions actively. Do not ban agreement measures; they suit coding-reliability approaches but not reflexive ones (Braun & Clarke 2019).

diagnostic.task: Ask the learner to talk through one findings paragraph and explain why they chose each extract and what their commentary adds.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Each extract is chosen to evidence a stated claim, commentary interprets rather than repeats, and divergent cases are mentioned.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Claims are present but commentary mostly paraphrases the extracts, or extract choice is not explained.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Extracts are presented without claims or commentary, or the learner cannot explain their selection.

guidance.contextNotes: UG qualitative projects tend to be small and may focus on presenting a few themes clearly. PGT dissertations in education, health and social sciences frequently use thematic analysis and merge findings with discussion. PGR writers must align reporting with a specific methodology, which may be phenomenological, ethnographic or discourse-analytic, and handle longer findings chapters.
reviewNotes: braunclarke2019 is a proposed reference (see proposedReferences), added in response to R6-23; if it is not accepted, remove the sentence on reflexive thematic analysis and the third difficulty's citation.

guidance.summary: Discussion sections have been modelled as cycles of moves: Hopkins and Dudley-Evans (1988) identified a sequence including statement of result, (un)expected outcome, reference to previous research, explanation, deduction and recommendation, recurring for each finding, and Yang and Allison (2003) described related moves in applied linguistics. Basturkmen (2009) found that published articles developed commentary on results more extensively than master's dissertations, for instance by offering and evaluating alternative explanations, which identifies a concrete target for postgraduate teaching. Swales and Feak (2012) provide practice in calibrating claims at the level of generality the data support.

activities.title: Cycle mapping
learnerActions: Annotate a discussion from your field for statement, comparison with literature, explanation and implication
Draw the cycles as a flow diagram
Draft your own discussion as a sequence of cycles, one per key finding
activities.intendedInsight: Discussions are built from repeated, finding-led cycles rather than from a single summary followed by implications.
activities.rationale: The cyclical move structure described by Hopkins and Dudley-Evans (1988) is a usable planning device.

activities.title: Alternative explanations
learnerActions: Choose one unexpected finding from your study
List at least three possible explanations, including methodological ones
Write a paragraph that weighs them using evidence and hedging
Compare your paragraph with an expert example that evaluates alternatives
activities.intendedInsight: Considering and weighing alternatives makes interpretation more credible than asserting a single explanation.
activities.rationale: Basturkmen (2009) identifies the development of alternative explanations as a difference between expert and student commentary.

difficulties.pattern: My discussion repeats my results and then says what future research should do.
difficulties.revealedBy: Discussions with few citations, no explanations of findings and generic implications.
difficulties.response: Use cycle mapping and require each finding to be compared with at least one previous study and explained. Do not respond by asking for a longer discussion; the issue is function, not length.

difficulties.pattern: My findings prove that the theory is correct.
difficulties.revealedBy: Boosted claims, generalisation beyond the sample and no mention of alternative explanations or limitations.
difficulties.response: Work through claim calibration with the learner's own sentences: what does the design allow, for whom, under what conditions? Avoid over-correcting into hedging every clause.

difficulties.pattern: Unexpected results are mistakes, so I mention them briefly or leave them out.
difficulties.revealedBy: Unexpected findings are omitted, apologised for or explained away without evidence.
difficulties.response: Present unexpected findings as a legitimate and often valuable part of discussions, and model language for treating them as findings to explain.

diagnostic.task: Ask the learner to pick their most important finding and say, in two minutes, how it relates to previous research and why it might have occurred.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Relates the finding to specific previous studies, proposes and weighs explanations, and states a calibrated implication.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Relates the finding to previous research but offers one explanation only, or makes uncalibrated claims.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Restates the finding without comparison or explanation.

guidance.contextNotes: UG reports often need a short discussion with comparison to the literature and limitations. PGT dissertations are frequently weakest in the discussion, so it deserves sustained attention. PGR writers handle multiple findings, theoretical contributions and examiners' expectations of originality, and may write a separate general discussion chapter.

guidance.summary: Limitations writing is an exercise in calibrated evaluation, not confession. Yang and Allison (2003) identify an evaluating-the-study move, covering limitations and significance, in the closing sections of applied linguistics articles, and Swales and Feak (2012) treat limitation statements as part of positioning a study's claims. Hyland (1998) shows how hedging allows writers to qualify commitment while protecting their claims. Teach learners to select consequential limitations, to state their effects and to frame them with concessive moves that keep the contribution intact.

activities.title: Limitation, effect, response
learnerActions: List every limitation of your study you can think of
Keep only those that affect how a reader should interpret your findings
For each, write one sentence on its likely effect and one on mitigation or future work
Compare your version with the limitation statements of two published studies in your field
activities.intendedInsight: Useful limitations are specific to the study and tell the reader how to read the findings.
activities.rationale: The evaluating-the-study move (Yang & Allison 2003) combines limitation with significance; structuring each limitation as effect plus response operationalises this.

activities.title: Tone calibration
learnerActions: Read three versions of the same limitation: apologetic, dismissive and calibrated
Identify the language that creates each tone (apology, minimisers, concessive structures, hedges)
Rewrite one of your own limitation statements in the calibrated style
activities.intendedInsight: Language choices determine whether a limitation weakens the study or demonstrates the writer's command of it.
activities.rationale: Hedging and concession shape commitment without retraction (Hyland 1998); contrasting versions makes the effect noticeable.

difficulties.pattern: This study has many limitations. The sample was small. The time was short. I apologise for these weaknesses.
difficulties.revealedBy: Long, generic, apologetic lists, often unconnected to the specific findings.
difficulties.response: Reframe limitations as evidence of methodological awareness, not as admissions of failure, and ask for the effect of each one on interpretation. Avoid telling the learner to omit limitations; examiners expect them.

difficulties.pattern: If I mention limitations, examiners will mark me down, so I add one sentence at the end.
difficulties.revealedBy: Missing or token limitations sections, even where a design has obvious constraints.
difficulties.response: Show marking criteria and examiners' reports that reward critical evaluation of one's own study, and discuss how unacknowledged limitations invite criticism.

diagnostic.task: Ask the learner to name the single most important limitation of their study and explain how it affects one specific finding.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Names a consequential limitation, explains its likely effect on a specific finding and suggests a mitigation or future direction.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Names a relevant limitation but cannot say how it affects the findings, or names only a generic one.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Cannot identify a limitation, or lists generic weaknesses unrelated to the design.

guidance.contextNotes: UG report criteria often require limitations explicitly, and short generic statements are common. At PGT, limitations are part of demonstrating criticality in the discussion. At PGR, limitations are scrutinised in the viva and by reviewers, and they must be consistent across thesis chapters and derived articles.

guidance.summary: Claiming contribution combines promotion with calibration. Hyland (2001) found that self-mention in research articles is concentrated where writers make claims and present their own contribution, and that it is more frequent in the humanities and social sciences than in the sciences, while Hyland (2005) describes how stance resources position claims relative to readers. Kamler and Thomson (2014) and W. L. Belcher (2019) both press novice writers to state the 'so what' of their work explicitly. Teach contribution statements as short, revisable texts that are linked to the niche and calibrated to the evidence.

activities.title: Contribution sentence drafting
learnerActions: Write one sentence stating what your study adds and one stating why it matters
Label the contribution type (empirical, methodological, theoretical, contextual or practical)
Check it against your niche statement and revise until they match
Test the sentences on a peer from outside your field
activities.intendedInsight: A contribution is only convincing if it answers the niche and can be stated plainly.
activities.rationale: Kamler and Thomson (2014) and W. L. Belcher (2019) both treat explicit articulation of the argument and its significance as central to successful research writing.

activities.title: Self-mention and stance survey
learnerActions: Collect contribution statements from ten articles in your target journals
Note the use of self-mention, boosters, hedges and evaluative adjectives
Decide what level of promotion is conventional in your field and revise your statement accordingly
activities.intendedInsight: Fields differ in how openly writers promote their contribution; matching the convention avoids both arrogance and invisibility.
activities.rationale: Hyland's (2001, 2005) findings on disciplinary variation in self-mention and stance support a field-specific approach.

difficulties.pattern: This is the first study ever to investigate this important topic, and it will revolutionise the field.
difficulties.revealedBy: Unsupported 'first', 'novel' and 'revolutionary' claims, boosted language and contributions disconnected from evidence.
difficulties.response: Ask the learner to point to the evidence for each element of the claim, then rewrite it in bounded terms. Do not ban promotional language altogether; teach calibrated promotion.

difficulties.pattern: It is not my place to say my work is original; the examiners will decide.
difficulties.revealedBy: No explicit contribution statement anywhere, or one hidden in heavy hedges and impersonal constructions.
difficulties.response: Explain that examiners and reviewers expect writers to state their contribution, and show examples of confident but measured statements. Discuss self-mention as a disciplinary choice rather than arrogance; reluctance to claim originality is common among novice writers of all backgrounds.

diagnostic.task: Ask the learner: 'In two sentences, what does your thesis add that we did not know before?'
diagnostic.strongResponse: States a specific, typed contribution, links it to a gap in the field and calibrates its scope.
diagnostic.partialResponse: States a topic-level contribution ('it adds to our understanding of X') or overstates its novelty.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Describes what the study did rather than what it adds, or cannot answer.

guidance.contextNotes: At PGT, the contribution may be modest and contextual, and the main need is to state it at all. At PGR, originality is an explicit examination criterion and must be argued throughout the thesis, in articles and in the viva.

guidance.summary: Conclusions in research writing do more than summarise. Yang and Allison (2003) describe conclusion moves in applied linguistics articles including summarising the study, evaluating it and deducing from the research, such as recommending further research and drawing pedagogic implications. For theses, Bunton (2005) distinguishes conclusions focused on the thesis itself from those oriented to the field. Teach learners to answer their research questions, articulate contribution and derive implications explicitly from findings, with genre-appropriate length.

activities.title: Question-answer check
learnerActions: Copy your research questions to the top of your draft conclusion
Highlight the sentence that answers each one
Add answers for any question not addressed, using the same key terms
Remove chapter-by-chapter summary that does not contribute to an answer
activities.intendedInsight: A conclusion is judged by whether it answers the questions the text set out to address.
activities.rationale: Summarising and evaluating moves (Yang & Allison 2003) work only when tied to the study's stated aims.

activities.title: Implication tracing
learnerActions: List each implication and recommendation in your conclusion
Draw an arrow from each to the finding that supports it
Rewrite or delete implications with no supporting finding
Make each future-research recommendation specific about focus, population or design
activities.intendedInsight: Implications must be grounded in findings, and recommendations for research are more convincing when specific.
activities.rationale: Thesis conclusions vary in orientation (Bunton 2005); tracing ensures that whatever the orientation, claims remain grounded.

difficulties.pattern: My conclusion repeats my abstract and ends with 'more research is needed'.
difficulties.revealedBy: Conclusions with no explicit answers, contribution or specific implications.
difficulties.response: Use the question–answer check and implication tracing. Do not just ask for more content; ask for the functional moves that are missing.

difficulties.pattern: New ideas and new literature appear for the first time in the conclusion.
difficulties.revealedBy: Conclusions introducing new findings, concepts or citations not discussed earlier.
difficulties.response: Help the learner move new material into the discussion or remove it, and reserve the conclusion for consolidating what has been established.

diagnostic.task: Ask the learner to read their conclusion and say which sentences answer which research questions and which state the contribution.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Points to explicit answers for every question, a contribution statement and implications linked to findings.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Answers some questions but implications are generic or the contribution is implicit.
diagnostic.gapResponse: The conclusion summarises content without answers, contribution or implications.

guidance.contextNotes: Many UG reports merge conclusions with the discussion. PGT dissertations usually have a separate conclusion chapter with recommendations. PGR thesis conclusions must synthesise across chapters, articulate contribution to knowledge and anticipate examiners' questions, and article conclusions follow journal norms that may omit a separate section.

guidance.summary: Abstracts are highly conventional and highly visible. Santos (1996) described a five-move structure for applied linguistics article abstracts (situating the research, presenting it, describing the methodology, summarising results and discussing the research), and Swales and Feak (2009) offer graded tasks across abstract types, including the distinction between informative and indicative abstracts. Student abstracts use similar moves but are read by markers checking that the writer can represent the work accurately and concisely, whereas research abstracts are also promotional texts in which writers present themselves as credible insiders, with disciplinary variation in which moves are included (Hyland 2004). Kamler and Thomson (2014) use abstract writing as a 'tiny text' that helps doctoral writers clarify their argument. Teach abstracts both as a genre, calibrated to local exemplars, and as a thinking tool.

activities.title: Move census
learnerActions: Collect eight to ten abstracts from your department, programme or target journal
Label each sentence by move and note which moves are present, absent or combined
Note tense, voice and the specificity of results statements
Draft your abstract to match the most common pattern, then justify any deviation
activities.intendedInsight: Abstract conventions are specific to journals and fields, and results are usually stated concretely.
activities.rationale: Move analysis (Santos 1996; Swales & Feak 2009) and disciplinary variation (Hyland 2004) suggest calibrating to a local corpus rather than a generic template.

activities.title: From indicative to informative
learnerActions: Read an abstract that says what the report 'will discuss' without stating results
Rewrite it so that it states the actual findings and conclusion
Compare which version better serves a marker, an examiner or a reader deciding whether to read on
activities.intendedInsight: Informative abstracts state findings; indicative abstracts only describe topics.
activities.rationale: The distinction between informative and indicative abstracts is a standard element of abstract instruction (Swales & Feak 2009).

activities.title: Abstract as argument test
learnerActions: Write a short abstract for your project early in the writing process
Exchange with a peer who states, in one sentence, what they think your argument is
Revise the abstract until the peer's sentence matches your intention
Revisit the abstract each time a chapter is completed
activities.intendedInsight: If the argument cannot be stated in an abstract, the text's argument may not yet be clear.
activities.rationale: Kamler and Thomson (2014) use abstract writing as a tool for doctoral writers to articulate their argument and contribution.

difficulties.pattern: The results will be discussed and implications will be considered.
difficulties.revealedBy: Indicative abstracts that describe content, or read like an introduction or table of contents, without stating findings or conclusions.
difficulties.response: Contrast indicative and informative abstracts and require at least one specific results statement. Avoid generalising: some genres, such as some humanities abstracts and conference proposals, legitimately differ.

difficulties.pattern: Half the abstract is background, and the method and results are squeezed into one sentence at the end.
difficulties.revealedBy: Disproportionate Move 1, often copied from the introduction.
difficulties.response: Have the learner allocate word counts per move before drafting, using exemplars as a guide.

difficulties.pattern: Inconsistent or unmotivated tense shifts between moves.
difficulties.revealedBy: Methods in the present and conclusions in the past, or random alternation within a move.
difficulties.response: Show the typical tense pattern by move and the reasons for it, noting that local conventions differ. Do not present one pattern as a rule for every field.

diagnostic.task: Ask the learner to write a 100-word abstract of a short article they have read, in ten minutes, without looking back at the original abstract.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Includes purpose, method, specific findings and a conclusion in proportion, with appropriate tense.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Includes most moves but results are vague or background is disproportionate.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Writes an introduction-like summary of the topic with no findings.

guidance.contextNotes: On postgraduate pre-sessionals, abstracts are written for extended projects and posters; undergraduate-entry courses that set an abstract can use the same core moves without the research-article emphasis. In-sessional UG learners write abstracts for final-year projects, lab reports and posters, often after drafting the full text. PGT learners write dissertation abstracts, sometimes structured, and abstracts for student conferences. PGR learners write thesis abstracts within institutional word limits and article abstracts that must match journal formats, including structured abstracts in health and some social sciences.
reviewNotes: Review response: R1-15 merged grp.student-abstract into this topic. Its moves, tense guidance, indicative-versus-informative activity and student contexts are incorporated here, and the range is widened to B2–C1.

guidance.summary: Paltridge (2002) identified four broad thesis types, traditional simple, traditional complex, topic-based and compilations of research papers, and found that published advice to thesis writers often described only the traditional simple type. Paltridge and Starfield (2020) extend this to guidance on choosing and planning structures, including publication-based theses, and Swales (2004) discusses the PhD dissertation as a research genre whose form has changed over time. Teaching should start from departmental theses and regulations, making the range of legitimate structures visible and linking the choice to the research design.

activities.title: Thesis repository survey
learnerActions: Download the tables of contents of five recent theses from your department
Classify each by macrostructure type
Note chapter titles, relative lengths and where literature and theory appear
Present to a mixed-discipline group and compare
activities.intendedInsight: There are several legitimate thesis structures, and the department's own practice is the most relevant guide.
activities.rationale: Paltridge's (2002) finding that published advice under-represents actual variety supports analysis of local theses rather than reliance on generic guides.

activities.title: Chapter purpose map
learnerActions: Draft a chapter plan listing each chapter's purpose and main claim
Show how each chapter connects to the research questions
For a publication-based thesis, plan the framing and linking chapters
Review the plan with your supervisor against the regulations
activities.intendedInsight: The macrostructure should express the thesis argument, not only the sequence of research activities.
activities.rationale: Paltridge and Starfield (2020) recommend planning chapters around the overall argument and the examiner's reading of the whole thesis.

difficulties.pattern: A thesis is just a very long dissertation with the same chapters.
difficulties.revealedBy: Plans that copy a master's dissertation structure regardless of whether the research has several studies or is theory-led.
difficulties.response: Show alternative structures from the department and ask the learner to justify their choice by the shape of the research.

difficulties.pattern: My chapters follow the order in which I did the work, so the argument only becomes clear at the end.
difficulties.revealedBy: Chapter plans organised by the chronology of fieldwork or experiments, with key concepts introduced late and conclusions that surprise the reader.
difficulties.response: Ask the learner to write the thesis argument in five sentences and to reorder chapters so that each sentence has a home. Keep chronology where it serves the argument.

diagnostic.task: Ask the learner to describe their thesis structure and explain why it suits their research.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Names a recognised structure, explains how it fits the design and argument, and shows awareness of regulations.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Has a reasonable plan but cannot justify it beyond 'this is the usual structure'.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Has no plan or applies an unsuitable structure without awareness of alternatives.

guidance.contextNotes: This is a PGR topic: master's dissertation structures are usually prescribed by the programme and are covered by the dissertation topic in Academic Genres. At PGR, learners may choose among structures; publication-based theses are increasingly common in some countries and fields, with institution-specific rules, and practice-based and professional doctorates have their own formats.
reviewNotes: Review response: R1-15 retagged this topic to PGR only, and R6-22 softened its dependency on IMRaD. Detailed guidance on integrating papers has moved to res.publication-based-thesis.

guidance.summary: In long texts, metatext operates above the paragraph: Bunton (1999) describes higher-level metatext in PhD theses that refers to chapters and to the thesis as a whole, and Hyland (2005) places frame markers, endophoric markers and code glosses within the interactive resources writers use to guide readers. Paltridge and Starfield (2020) discuss chapter introductions and conclusions as structural signposts. Teach metatext as reader guidance that should be accurate, proportionate and revised as the thesis changes.

activities.title: Skeleton read-through
learnerActions: Extract all chapter introductions and conclusions from a model thesis
Read them in sequence and summarise the thesis argument
Repeat the exercise with your own draft
Identify where the argument breaks down and revise the metatext
activities.intendedInsight: Chapter openings and closings carry the thesis argument for readers who navigate rather than read straight through.
activities.rationale: Higher-level metatext guides readers across the thesis (Bunton 1999; Hyland 2005); reading it alone tests whether it does that job.

activities.title: Metatext density check
learnerActions: Highlight all metatext in one chapter
Count instances per page and compare with a model thesis in your field
Remove redundant previews and repetitive formulae
Check every cross-reference against the current chapter numbering
activities.intendedInsight: Too little metatext leaves readers lost, while too much pads the text and can read as uncertain.
activities.rationale: Metadiscourse varies across fields and genres (Hyland 2005), so a local comparison is a better guide than a fixed rule.

difficulties.pattern: Every chapter begins 'In this chapter, I will…' followed by a list of section headings.
difficulties.revealedBy: Formulaic previews that duplicate the table of contents and do not state purpose or relation to the argument.
difficulties.response: Ask the learner to state why the chapter is there before what it contains, and to vary language. Avoid forbidding previews, which are conventional and useful.

difficulties.pattern: Previews and cross-references refer to chapters that have since moved or been cut.
difficulties.revealedBy: Inaccurate 'see Chapter 4' references and previews that no longer match content.
difficulties.response: Recommend automatic cross-referencing in word processors and a final metatext check as a distinct editing pass.

diagnostic.task: Ask the learner to read aloud the first and last paragraphs of one chapter and say how they connect to the chapters before and after.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Paragraphs state the chapter's purpose and contribution and link explicitly to adjacent chapters and the research questions.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Paragraphs preview or summarise content but do not link to the wider argument.
diagnostic.gapResponse: No chapter introduction or conclusion, or paragraphs that are unrelated to the thesis argument.

guidance.contextNotes: PGT dissertations benefit from chapter introductions and conclusions but on a smaller scale. At PGR, metatext is essential to readability and is often added or revised in the final stages, and publication-based theses need linking text between papers.

guidance.summary: Proposals are persuasive, promissory genres read by evaluators under time pressure. Connor and Mauranen (1999) analysed EU research grant proposals and identified moves such as territory, gap, goal, means, reporting previous research, achievements, benefits, importance and competence claims, showing that proposals combine research-article moves with promotional ones; doctoral proposals share many of these moves, with more emphasis on design and feasibility. Creswell and Creswell (2018) give templates for qualitative, quantitative and mixed-methods proposals, and Paltridge and Starfield (2020) address doctoral proposals. Teach learners to analyse the specific template and criteria they face and to make alignment and feasibility visible.

activities.title: Criteria mapping
learnerActions: Obtain the assessment criteria for your proposal (admission, confirmation or funder)
Map each criterion to the section of your draft that addresses it
Identify criteria addressed weakly or not at all
Revise those sections and ask a peer to score the draft against the criteria
activities.intendedInsight: Proposals are evaluated against explicit criteria, and writers should address these visibly.
activities.rationale: Connor and Mauranen (1999) show that proposals include moves such as benefits and competence claims that respond to evaluators' needs rather than to purely academic conventions.

activities.title: Promissory language workshop
learnerActions: Collect future and conditional forms from funded proposals (will, aims to, is expected to, would enable)
Compare with language from completed-research articles
Revise your proposal to commit clearly to actions while hedging expected outcomes
activities.intendedInsight: Proposals commit firmly to what the researcher will do but calibrate claims about what will be found.
activities.rationale: Proposal templates (Creswell & Creswell 2018) separate planned procedures from anticipated outcomes, which calls for different degrees of commitment.

difficulties.pattern: My proposal explains the topic in depth but the methods are a paragraph and there is no timeline.
difficulties.revealedBy: Proposals that resemble essays, with extensive background and little design or feasibility detail.
difficulties.response: Use the criteria map to show reviewers' priorities, and ask for a Gantt-style timeline and a risk table.

difficulties.pattern: My study will prove that…
difficulties.revealedBy: Predetermined conclusions and boosted claims about outcomes of research not yet done.
difficulties.response: Distinguish what the researcher will do from what they expect to find, and practise hypothesis and expectation language.

diagnostic.task: Ask the learner to give a 90-second pitch of their proposal covering the problem, aims, approach, feasibility and significance.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Covers all elements concisely, with aims and approach clearly aligned and significance tailored to the audience.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Covers problem and aims well but is vague on approach or feasibility.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Describes the topic without stating aims, approach or significance.

guidance.contextNotes: On postgraduate pre-sessionals, prospective doctoral students draft or revise the proposal on which admission or supervision depends; prospective master's students usually write the student project proposal instead. PGT learners applying for doctoral study write admission proposals. At PGR, the proposal is revised during the first year and then feeds the confirmation or progression report and, later, funding applications, which have their own topics.
reviewNotes: Review response: R1-15 asks for a stage boundary with grp.project-proposal; the description now states it, and pre-sessional use is limited to the postgraduate stage for prospective doctoral students. Confirmation reports and grant applications have moved to res.progression-review and pub.funding-applications.

guidance.summary: Ethics documentation joins research integrity to plain-language writing. Creswell and Creswell (2018) set out ethical issues to anticipate at each stage of research, which can structure an application, and the Vitae RDF places ethics and research integrity within the professional conduct sub-domain (C1). For participant documents, the main EAP task is adapting register for a lay reader while preserving accuracy, which is mediation across audiences. Institutional templates take precedence and should be the starting point.

activities.title: Two-audience rewrite
learnerActions: Take a paragraph from your ethics application describing what participants will do
Rewrite it for a participant information sheet using plain language and direct address
Ask a peer outside your field to explain back what taking part involves
Revise any part they misunderstood
activities.intendedInsight: The same procedure must be described differently for a committee and for a participant, without loss of accuracy.
activities.rationale: Adapting register for a non-specialist audience is a mediation skill; comprehension checks with lay readers make clarity testable.

activities.title: Consistency audit
learnerActions: Place your methods description, ethics application and participant documents side by side
Check that sample, procedures, data storage and withdrawal arrangements match
Record and correct any discrepancies
activities.intendedInsight: Inconsistencies between documents can delay approval and raise integrity concerns later.
activities.rationale: Integrity requires that research is conducted as approved, which depends on consistent documentation (Vitae 2010, sub-domain C1).

difficulties.pattern: Participants will be informed that their data will be pseudonymised and stored in accordance with GDPR-compliant protocols.
difficulties.revealedBy: Participant sheets written in committee or legal register, with long sentences and technical terms.
difficulties.response: Model plain-language equivalents and use readability checks as a prompt for revision, not as a target. Keep required legal elements but explain them.

difficulties.pattern: Ethics is a bureaucratic hurdle, so I copy someone else's form and change the title.
difficulties.revealedBy: Applications that do not describe the actual study, and mismatched risks and procedures.
difficulties.response: Discuss the purpose of ethics review and the integrity implications of inaccurate applications.

diagnostic.task: Ask the learner to explain to you, as if you were a potential participant, what taking part in their study would involve and what happens to your data.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Explains clearly and accurately in plain language, including voluntariness, withdrawal and data handling.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Explains procedures but omits withdrawal or data use, or slips into technical language.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Cannot give a clear account, or relies on jargon.

guidance.contextNotes: UG dissertations involving human participants usually require departmental ethics approval with simplified forms. PGT dissertations often involve first full applications. PGR applications may be complex, multi-site or international and may involve translated participant documents.
reviewNotes: No source in the current bibliography addresses the readability of participant information sheets directly; a reference from research-ethics or health-communication literature would strengthen this topic.

guidance.summary: Supervision is a relationship mediated by talk and text, and it is often where tacit disciplinary expectations become visible.
