Belcher (1994) studied three advisor–student pairs and linked the more successful relationship to a more reciprocal, collaborative stance and shared understanding of the target discourse community. Kamler and Thomson (2014) and Paltridge and Starfield (2020) treat supervision as a site of writing pedagogy, and Carless and Boud (2018) show that taking up feedback requires appreciating it, making judgements, managing affect and acting. Teach explicit expectation-setting and feedback negotiation, and treat indirectness in supervisor comments as a pragmatic issue.

activities.title: Expectation-setting conversation
learnerActions: Complete an expectations checklist covering meeting frequency, draft turnaround, feedback type and communication channels
Discuss it with your supervisor and agree a short written summary
Review the summary at an agreed point
activities.intendedInsight: Making expectations explicit reduces misunderstandings that might otherwise be attributed to language or personality.
activities.rationale: Belcher (1994) shows that mismatched understandings can undermine supervisory relationships; making them explicit is a practical response.

activities.title: Decoding feedback comments
learnerActions: Collect anonymised supervisor comments from your drafts
Classify each as directive, suggestion, question or praise, and rate how indirect it is
Write a response log stating what you changed for each comment or why you did not
Discuss any comments you were unsure about at the next meeting
activities.intendedInsight: Hedged comments are usually requests, and a response log makes engagement with feedback visible.
activities.rationale: Carless and Boud (2018) identify making judgements and taking action as components of feedback literacy; a response log operationalises both.

difficulties.pattern: My supervisor said 'you might want to think about' restructuring, so it's optional.
difficulties.revealedBy: Hedged suggestions left unaddressed and surprise when the supervisor repeats them more forcefully.
difficulties.response: Discuss how indirectness in English academic feedback often encodes requests, and practise clarifying ('Would you like me to restructure this before the next draft?'). Note that this varies by individual supervisor and that many first-language English students misread hedged advice too; clarity is a shared responsibility, so where possible encourage supervisors to mark which suggestions are requirements.

difficulties.pattern: I send my supervisor a whole chapter with no note and then wait for weeks without asking when to expect comments.
difficulties.revealedBy: Feedback that does not address the learner's priorities, long waits and frustration on both sides.
difficulties.response: Practise covering notes that state the stage of the draft, two or three specific questions and a requested timescale, and agree expectations about turnaround early. Recognise that delays can have institutional causes such as supervisors' workloads, and make sure learners know the routes for raising concerns.

diagnostic.task: Ask the learner to draft the email they would send with their next chapter draft.
diagnostic.strongResponse: States the draft's stage, asks two or three specific questions, proposes a meeting and uses an appropriate register.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Sends the draft politely but with no specific questions or stage information.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Sends the draft with no context or with an inappropriate register or demand.

guidance.contextNotes: UG dissertation supervision is usually brief and structured. PGT supervision is time-limited, so efficient agendas and specific requests matter. At PGR, supervision is a multi-year relationship, often with co-supervisors and formal progress reviews, and expectations differ by country and institution.

guidance.summary: Kamler and Thomson (2014) reject the idea of 'writing up' at the end of research and treat writing as a way of doing research and of forming a scholarly identity, which supports writing from the start of a project. Self-regulation research (Zimmerman 2002) provides a cycle of forethought, performance and self-reflection that maps onto writing goals, monitoring and adjustment. Paltridge and Starfield (2020) discuss practical strategies for managing thesis writing. Writing groups and retreats are widely used in doctoral education; present them as options to try and evaluate, not as proven interventions.

activities.title: Writing log cycle
learnerActions: Set a weekly writing goal in terms of specific text
Log each session's time, output and obstacles
Review the log at the end of the week and adjust the next goal and strategy
Share one insight with a writing partner
activities.intendedInsight: Monitoring actual writing behaviour reveals patterns that intentions hide.
activities.rationale: The forethought–performance–reflection cycle of self-regulated learning (Zimmerman 2002) applied to writing.

activities.title: Writing group trial
learnerActions: Join or form a writing group that meets regularly for focused writing time
State a session goal at the start and report progress at the end
After four sessions, evaluate whether the group helps and adjust the format
activities.intendedInsight: Social structures can make writing regular and less isolating.
activities.rationale: Kamler and Thomson (2014) argue for social and pedagogical structures around doctoral writing; the specific format here is a proposal to test locally.

difficulties.pattern: I will start writing when I have finished reading and collecting data.
difficulties.revealedBy: Long periods with no written output and a last-minute writing crisis.
difficulties.response: Present writing as part of thinking and research (memos, draft sections, notes towards chapters). Avoid shaming; many writers have been taught that writing comes last.

difficulties.pattern: I keep rewriting the first chapter and never move on.
difficulties.revealedBy: Repeated versions of one section with little overall progress.
difficulties.response: Encourage separating generative drafting from revision, and set goals for new text. Refer to wellbeing services where anxiety is significant.

diagnostic.task: Ask the learner to describe a typical writing week and what they produced last week.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Describes a regular routine, text-specific goals and at least one support structure, and can name what was produced.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Writes regularly but with vague goals, or relies only on bursts before deadlines.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Has no routine or output and is postponing writing to a later stage.

guidance.contextNotes: PGT dissertation writing is compressed into a few months, so planning and routines matter most. PGR writing spans years, and sustained productivity, wellbeing and recovery from setbacks become central, often with institutional writing retreats and groups.

guidance.summary: Positionality writing draws on work on writer identity and self-mention. Ivanič (1998) distinguishes the autobiographical self, the discoursal self and the self as author, which helps writers separate useful reflexivity from personal narrative, and Tang and John (1999) and Hyland (2002) describe the roles authors take through first-person reference. Creswell and Creswell (2018) present reflexivity as a component of qualitative research reporting. Teach positionality statements as analytic, study-specific and linked to methodological decisions.

activities.title: From identity list to analytic statement
learnerActions: List aspects of your position relevant to the study (relationship to participants, language, professional role, theoretical commitments)
For each, write how it may have shaped access, data or interpretation
Note what you did about it
Draft a statement that keeps only the aspects that had consequences
activities.intendedInsight: Positionality is valuable when it explains effects and responses, not when it lists identity categories.
activities.rationale: Creswell and Creswell (2018) frame reflexivity in terms of how researcher background shapes interpretation, which this sequence makes explicit.

activities.title: First-person roles
learnerActions: Collect first-person uses from methodology and reflexivity sections in your field
Classify them by authorial role (representative, guide, recounter of procedures, opinion-holder, originator)
Check your own statement for the range of roles you use
activities.intendedInsight: First-person reference can perform different roles, and reflexive writing needs the more committed ones.
activities.rationale: Tang and John's (1999) typology of 'I' roles and Hyland's (2002) work on authorial identity support a role-based analysis.

difficulties.pattern: I was taught never to use 'I' in academic writing, so I write 'the researcher' throughout my positionality statement.
difficulties.revealedBy: Awkward third-person self-reference in sections where first person is conventional.
difficulties.response: Show field exemplars using 'I' in reflexive sections and discuss the myth of the absolute rule. Respect institutional or supervisory requirements where they genuinely differ.

difficulties.pattern: My positionality statement describes my life story and why I care about the topic.
difficulties.revealedBy: Biographical narratives with no link to methodological decisions or interpretation.
difficulties.response: Ask for each sentence 'So what for the study?' and cut or develop accordingly.

diagnostic.task: Ask the learner to explain how one aspect of their position might have affected one specific finding.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Names a specific aspect, explains a plausible effect on a specific finding and describes what was done about it.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Names a relevant aspect but the effect is general or no response is described.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Lists identity categories or describes personal motivation without consequences.

guidance.contextNotes: At PGT, positionality statements are mainly required in qualitative dissertations in education, health and social sciences. At PGR they are often integrated throughout the methodology and discussion and are probed in the viva. In many quantitative and experimental fields they are not expected.

guidance.summary: Hyland's (2004) analysis of dissertation acknowledgements identified a three-tier structure (reflecting, thanking and announcing moves) and showed the genre's role in self-presentation and academic networking. Article acknowledgements serve additional functions: disclosing funding and recognising contributors who do not meet authorship criteria (ICMJE, 2025; Brand et al., 2015). Teaching should combine move analysis with institutional and journal requirements and attention to confidentiality.

activities.title: Move analysis of acknowledgements
learnerActions: Analyse several thesis or dissertation acknowledgements from their field
Identify the moves and their order
Note variation in register and length
Draft their own acknowledgement
activities.intendedInsight: Acknowledgements follow recognisable conventions while allowing personal expression.
activities.rationale: Hyland (2004) identifies the moves of dissertation acknowledgements, providing a basis for analysis.

activities.title: Who goes where?
learnerActions: Sort a list of contributors into authors, acknowledged contributors and those not acknowledged
Justify decisions using ICMJE criteria or CRediT roles
Draft a funding statement
Compare decisions with peers
activities.intendedInsight: Acknowledgement and authorship are distinct, with ethical implications.
activities.rationale: Authorship criteria (ICMJE, 2025) and contributor role taxonomies (Brand et al., 2015) define who is acknowledged rather than listed as an author.

difficulties.pattern: Naming participants or organisations that were promised anonymity.
difficulties.revealedBy: Acknowledgements that identify research sites or participants by name.
difficulties.response: Check the consent and ethics documentation before naming anyone, and thank participants collectively where anonymity was promised.

difficulties.pattern: Register that is either extremely effusive or perfunctory.
difficulties.revealedBy: Very long, emotional acknowledgements or a single generic line.
difficulties.response: Show a range of models from the learner's field and institution and discuss audience.

difficulties.pattern: Offering authorship as a form of thanks, or acknowledging someone whose contribution merits authorship.
difficulties.revealedBy: Proposed author lists that include people who only provided resources, or acknowledgements of substantial intellectual contributors.
difficulties.response: Revisit authorship criteria and discuss with supervisors.

diagnostic.task: Give a list of contributors and ask the learner to decide who is acknowledged, who might be an author and how anonymous participants are thanked.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Correctly distinguishes authors and acknowledged contributors, includes funding details and protects anonymity.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Mostly correct but omits funding or names an anonymous participant.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Confuses authorship and acknowledgement or omits required elements.

guidance.contextNotes: UG and PGT dissertation acknowledgements are usually short and optional. PGR thesis acknowledgements are longer and more personal, and in theses by publication they sit alongside contribution statements for each paper. Article acknowledgements are formulaic and often accompany required funding and competing-interest statements. Conventions on how personal thesis acknowledgements may be vary across countries and institutions.
reviewNotes: Review response: R1-33 moved this topic from Academic Pragmatics (prg.acknowledgements) to Research Writing; it now links to ethics documentation and authorship as part of the thesis and article apparatus.

guidance.summary: Progression reviews are often the first formal assessment of a doctoral researcher's writing and of their ability to defend a design orally, but their form is set by local regulations rather than by a shared genre model, so teaching starts from the institution's documentation, criteria and, with permission, past reports. Kamler and Thomson (2014) treat early doctoral texts as both text work and identity work, and Paltridge and Starfield (2020) address the doctoral proposal from which these reports develop; together they support treating the report as an argued account of a developing project rather than a list of activities. The Vitae Researcher Development Framework (Vitae 2010) places project planning and risk management under research management (C2), which gives panels' feasibility questions a recognisable basis. Rehearsing the oral component with probing follow-up questions is a practitioner proposal, and anxiety about a high-stakes milestone should be acknowledged rather than dismissed.

activities.title: What has changed and why
learnerActions: List the differences between your original proposal and your current project: questions, design, sample, scope and timeline
For each change, write one or two sentences giving the reason and the evidence that prompted it
Draft the report's progress-and-revisions section from these notes
Ask a peer from another field whether each change reads as a reasoned decision or as drift
activities.intendedInsight: Panels expect projects to change; they assess whether changes are reasoned, evidenced and coherent with the aims.
activities.rationale: Presenting a revised design as argued development rather than as failure reflects the view of doctoral writing as ongoing text and identity work (Kamler & Thomson 2014); the activity is a practical proposal.

activities.title: Mock panel with follow-ups
learnerActions: Exchange reports in groups of three and prepare two feasibility questions and one design question for each other
Run ten-minute panels in which every first answer receives at least one follow-up question
Note which answers referred to specific evidence in the plan and which stayed general
Revise the timeline or risk table in response to the hardest question
activities.intendedInsight: Feasibility is shown through specific plans, contingencies and evidence, and panel questions are a resource for improving the plan.
activities.rationale: Panels typically probe research management, which the Vitae RDF describes in terms of project planning, delivery and risk (Vitae 2010); follow-up questions bring the rehearsal closer to the real event. This is a practitioner proposal, not a tested intervention.

difficulties.pattern: My report lists everything I did this year — courses, conferences, reading — so the panel can see I have worked hard.
difficulties.revealedBy: Activity-log reports with little about questions, design or findings and no argument that the project is on track.
difficulties.response: Show that panels judge the coherence and feasibility of the project, not effort. Ask the learner to open each section with a claim about the project and to use activities only as evidence; training records usually belong in a separate form or appendix.

difficulties.pattern: Changing my research questions will look like failure, so I keep the original ones even though my data no longer fit them.
difficulties.revealedBy: Questions that no longer match the design or preliminary findings, and evasive answers when the panel asks about the mismatch.
difficulties.response: Present revision as an expected part of doctoral research and model sentences that report a change with its reason. Do not push changes for their own sake; the aim is alignment between questions, design and data.

difficulties.pattern: The criteria, length and the panel's role differ from what other students told me, and nobody explained what the possible outcomes mean.
difficulties.revealedBy: Reports written to the wrong length or template, and candidates surprised by outcomes such as a deferred decision or a second review.
difficulties.response: Teachers should work from the current regulations and criteria with the learner, and graduate schools should publish exemplars and descriptions of outcomes. Learners can ask the supervisor or panel chair in writing what will be assessed. Candidates who need adjustments to the oral component, such as questions in advance or rest breaks, should arrange them through the institution's normal processes.

diagnostic.task: Ask the learner to explain in two minutes what has changed in their project since the proposal and why, then ask one follow-up question about feasibility.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Names specific changes with reasons grounded in the work, links them to the aims and answers the follow-up with concrete evidence such as dates, access arrangements or pilot results.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Describes changes accurately but gives reasons only in general terms, or answers the follow-up with reassurance rather than evidence.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Lists activities without identifying changes, or cannot connect the plan to the remaining time and resources.

guidance.contextNotes: This is a PGR topic, best taught in the months before the first formal review. UK institutions commonly hold a confirmation or upgrade review in the first year or so and annual reviews after that; Australian universities typically have a confirmation of candidature; in North America the comparable hurdles are usually qualifying or comprehensive examinations and a prospectus or proposal defence; in many continental European systems a first-year evaluation or individual study plan serves a similar purpose. Part-time, professional-doctorate and publication-based candidates often have different timings and components.
reviewNotes: No genre analysis of confirmation or progression reports is in the bibliography; the guidance relies on doctoral-writing handbooks and the Vitae RDF and should be checked against local regulations.

guidance.summary: Paltridge (2002) identified compilations of research papers as one of four broad thesis types and found that published advice for thesis writers seldom described them, and Paltridge and Starfield (2020) discuss how publication-based theses are framed and integrated. The integrative chapters must carry the argument of the whole thesis across papers written for different journals and readerships, so teaching concentrates on framing, linking and cross-paper synthesis, and on contribution statements that make the candidate's responsibility for co-authored work visible. Contributor-role taxonomies such as CRediT (Brand et al. 2015) can structure these statements, although institutions usually prescribe their own forms.

activities.title: Thread map
learnerActions: List your papers and write the one question each answers
Draw the relations between them (extends, tests, applies, explains) and name the overarching problem they share
Draft the paragraph of your introduction that explains this structure to an examiner
Check that your concluding chapter answers the overarching problem, not only each paper's question
activities.intendedInsight: The integrating argument has to be made explicit because the papers were written to stand alone.
activities.rationale: Paltridge and Starfield (2020) stress that a publication-based thesis must still read as a coherent whole; mapping the relations between papers makes that argument plannable. The activity is a practical proposal.

activities.title: Contribution statements
learnerActions: Collect contribution statements from theses by publication in your institution
List each author's contributions to one of your papers using CRediT roles
Draft your contribution statement in the institution's required form
Check the statement with your co-authors
activities.intendedInsight: Contribution statements must be accurate, agreed with co-authors and specific enough for examiners to judge the candidate's own work.
activities.rationale: CRediT (Brand et al. 2015) provides a shared vocabulary for contributor roles, which helps make individual contributions explicit.

difficulties.pattern: In a thesis by publication, I just staple my papers together.
difficulties.revealedBy: Minimal introductory and concluding chapters, literature reviews repeated across papers and no linking text.
difficulties.response: Discuss examiners' expectations of coherence across the whole thesis and the institution's rules on framing chapters. Ask for a written account of how the papers relate before any integrative text is drafted.

difficulties.pattern: My concluding chapter summarises paper 1, then paper 2, then paper 3.
difficulties.revealedBy: Conclusions made of paper-by-paper summaries, with no cross-paper synthesis and no statement of the thesis's overall contribution.
difficulties.response: Ask the learner to write three claims that can only be supported by combining papers, then build the conclusion around them. Do not insist on removing all summary; brief reminders help examiners.

difficulties.pattern: The rules on co-authored papers, the status of submitted papers and reproducing published text are unclear, and my supervisors disagree.
difficulties.revealedBy: Late discovery that a paper does not count, that a publisher's permission is needed or that contribution forms are required.
difficulties.response: Point learners to the current regulations and publishers' author-reuse policies early, and encourage graduate schools to publish clear guidance and exemplars. Learners should record decisions about paper status and co-authorship with their supervisors in writing.

diagnostic.task: Ask the learner to explain, in under two minutes, how their papers together answer one overarching research problem.
diagnostic.strongResponse: States a single problem, names the role of each paper in addressing it and identifies a contribution that emerges only from the set.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Describes each paper clearly but links them chronologically or by topic without an overarching argument.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Cannot state a shared problem, or describes the papers as independent projects.

guidance.contextNotes: This is a PGR topic. Theses by publication are common in the Nordic countries, the Netherlands and Australia and in many science, health and engineering fields, and are increasingly offered elsewhere, including in the social sciences; some systems require papers to be published, others accept submitted or publishable papers. Professional doctorates and retrospective PhDs by published works have their own requirements, and candidates should find out how examiners are briefed to judge coherence.

guidance.summary: PRISMA 2020 (Page et al. 2021) sets out the items a systematic review report should contain, including full search strategies, a flow diagram of study selection and the methods used to assess risk of bias and certainty, and many journals and examiners use it as a checklist. Arksey and O'Malley (2005) proposed a framework for scoping studies that map the extent and nature of research rather than appraising and pooling it, which changes what the report must say. Greenhalgh (2019) explains how health readers appraise systematic reviews, which helps writers anticipate what a critical reader will check. EAP teaching concentrates on the reporting language (precise past-tense procedure, transparent numbers, cross-study synthesis and calibrated conclusions) and on matching the review type to the question; review methods themselves are taught by subject specialists and librarians.

activities.title: Checklist-led reverse engineering
learnerActions: Choose a published review in your field that reports following PRISMA 2020 or one of its extensions
Locate where each checklist item for the methods and results is reported
Mark the sentence patterns used to report searches, selection and appraisal
Draft the same sections for your own review protocol
activities.intendedInsight: Reporting guidelines specify content; published reviews show how that content is phrased and placed.
activities.rationale: Page et al. (2021) present PRISMA 2020 as reporting guidance; analysing exemplars against it connects the checklist to the language that realises it.

activities.title: From study-by-study to synthesis
learnerActions: Take a results draft that summarises included studies one at a time
Group the findings by outcome, theme or direction of effect in a table
Rewrite one paragraph so that it opens with a claim about the body of evidence and cites studies in support
Add a sentence on the quality or consistency of that evidence
activities.intendedInsight: A review synthesis makes claims about a body of evidence, qualified by its quality, rather than describing studies in turn.
activities.rationale: Synthesis across studies and calibration to the certainty of evidence are central reporting items in PRISMA 2020 (Page et al. 2021); the activity is a practitioner proposal adapted from teaching synthesis paragraphs.

difficulties.pattern: A systematic review is just a literature review with more sources.
difficulties.revealedBy: Protocols with no explicit eligibility criteria or search strategy, and reports that select studies to support a position.
difficulties.response: Contrast the purposes and reporting requirements of narrative, scoping and systematic reviews using one example of each from the learner's field. Do not present the systematic review as superior; the right type depends on the question.

difficulties.pattern: Study A found…; Study B found…; Study C found…, followed by a one-line conclusion.
difficulties.revealedBy: Results organised study by study, with appraisal reported separately and not used in the synthesis.
difficulties.response: Use a findings-by-study matrix to plan claims across studies, and require each synthesis paragraph to say how strong the evidence behind its claim is.

difficulties.pattern: My supervisor asked for a 'systematic review', but there is no time or second reviewer for screening.
difficulties.revealedBy: Reviews labelled systematic that lack the procedures the label implies, and examiners questioning the method.
difficulties.response: Help the learner and supervisor agree an honest label, such as a scoping or rapid review or a review with a systematic search, and report the procedures actually used. Programmes that set review-based dissertations should state which review type and procedures they expect.

diagnostic.task: Ask the learner to write three sentences reporting a database search and its results for a review they are planning or have read.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Names databases and dates, says where the full strategy is available and gives the numbers retrieved, screened and included, in precise past-tense prose.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Gives sources and numbers but omits dates or the screening procedure, or reports the procedure vaguely.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Describes the topic of the search without details that would allow it to be repeated.

guidance.contextNotes: At PGT, review-based dissertations are common in health, education, psychology and management, often as scoping or rapid reviews with limited resources, so honesty about the review type matters more than full systematic procedures. At PGR, a systematic or scoping review is often the first paper or chapter, with a registered protocol (for example on PROSPERO or the Open Science Framework) and full reporting to a guideline. Fields differ: software engineering has its own guidelines for systematic literature reviews, and qualitative evidence syntheses have specific reporting standards.
reviewNotes: Review response: R6-02 also asks for dhl.critical-appraisal to be narrowed to single-study appraisal and its PRISMA material moved here; that edit belongs to the Disciplinary Literacies group. This topic depends softly on dhl.critical-appraisal.

guidance.summary: Creswell and Creswell (2018) treat instrument design as part of research design, linking items to variables and research questions and recommending piloting. Item-writing guidelines developed for tests (Haladyna et al. 2002) share several principles that carry over to questionnaires, such as keeping each item focused, using vocabulary suited to the respondents and avoiding negative wording, although they were written for multiple-choice assessment rather than surveys. For EAP the topic is a language problem as much as a methods one: precision, neutrality, presupposition and register decide whether participants answer the question the researcher intended. Teach it through diagnosis and rewriting of flawed items and through think-aloud piloting, in which a few people like the participants say how they understand each item.

activities.title: Item clinic
learnerActions: Sort a set of flawed items by problem: double-barrelled, leading, presupposing, negative, vague quantifier or jargon
Rewrite each item and compare rewrites in pairs
Check each rewrite against the research question it is meant to serve
Apply the same checks to your own draft instrument
activities.intendedInsight: Most item problems are visible in the wording and can be fixed before data collection.
activities.rationale: Guidance on focused, positively worded items (Haladyna et al. 2002) and on aligning instruments with variables (Creswell & Creswell 2018) can be turned into a checklist; the activity is a practitioner proposal.

activities.title: Think-aloud pilot
learnerActions: Recruit two or three people similar to your participants
Ask them to read each item aloud and say what they think it asks and how they would answer
Record misunderstandings and hesitations
Revise the items and note the changes for your methods section
activities.intendedInsight: Researchers cannot judge clarity from their own reading; participants' interpretations reveal ambiguity.
activities.rationale: Piloting is a standard recommendation in research design texts (Creswell & Creswell 2018); asking pilot participants to say how they read each item makes ambiguity visible.

difficulties.pattern: Do you agree that the new library services are useful and easy to access?
difficulties.revealedBy: Items that ask two things at once, presuppose an answer or invite agreement.
difficulties.response: Teach the checks one at a time and have learners mark each item against them. Do not ban agree–disagree formats; teach when they suit the construct and how to balance them.

difficulties.pattern: My participants are students like me, so they will understand my questions.
difficulties.revealedBy: Items that use disciplinary terms or the researcher's own concepts, and no pilot reported.
difficulties.response: Require a pilot with at least two people outside the research team and a short record of what changed. Where participants will answer in another language, plan translation and checking with a fluent speaker.

difficulties.pattern: Some of my items do not measure anything my research questions ask about, and one construct has no items at all.
difficulties.revealedBy: Questionnaires with items that cannot be traced to any construct, and constructs with no items.
difficulties.response: Have the learner build an alignment table running from research question to construct to items before revising any wording.

diagnostic.task: Ask the learner to write one questionnaire item and one interview prompt for a stated research question and to say who will answer them.
diagnostic.strongResponse: The item is single-focus, neutral and in the participants' language with suitable response options; the prompt is open with a planned probe; both are clearly linked to the question.
diagnostic.partialResponse: One of the two is well formed, but the other leads, asks two things or uses jargon.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Both are leading or yes/no and cannot be traced to the research question.

guidance.contextNotes: On postgraduate pre-sessionals, short questionnaire or interview projects make this topic useful when an instrument forms part of the assessed project; undergraduate-entry courses with survey projects can use a simplified version of the item checks. UG and PGT dissertations in the social sciences, education, business and health often rely on self-designed instruments with limited piloting. At PGR, wording interacts with validated scales, translation and adaptation across languages, and ethics committee review of instruments.
reviewNotes: The bibliography has no dedicated source on questionnaire or interview design; haladyna2002 is cited only for item-writing principles that carry over from test design.

guidance.summary: Research on international teaching assistants shows that students' comprehension judgements depend on more than the speaker's language: Rubin (1992) found that undergraduates who believed a recorded lecture was given by an Asian instructor rated the speaker as more accented and scored lower on comprehension than those who heard the same recording attributed to a white instructor. Pickering (2001) found differences in tone choice between international and US teaching assistants that affected how information and rapport were signalled in class. Written feedback on student work can be framed by principles of good feedback practice (Nicol & Macfarlane-Dick 2006), such as clarifying what good performance is and giving information students can act on. The Vitae Researcher Development Framework (Vitae 2010) places teaching within engagement and impact. Teach explanation, questioning and feedback language explicitly, and address listener expectations and institutional support alongside the teaching assistant's own speech.

activities.title: Micro-teach with checks
learnerActions: Choose a concept or procedure that first-year students often find difficult
Plan a three-part explanation: link to what students know, explain with an example, then check understanding with a question that requires students to use the idea rather than 'Is that clear?'
Deliver it to peers and receive feedback on organisation, examples and checking
Teach it again with one change
activities.intendedInsight: Clear teaching talk depends on organisation and checking as much as on pronunciation.
activities.rationale: Rubin (1992) and Pickering (2001) suggest that comprehension in international teaching assistants' classes depends on listener expectations and on discourse-level features such as tone choice, not only on individual sounds; micro-teaching targets the features the teaching assistant controls. This is a practitioner proposal.

activities.title: Feedback calibration
learnerActions: Mark the same anonymised student answer independently using the module criteria
Compare marks and written comments in a group
Rewrite comments so that each refers to a criterion and suggests a next step
Agree how to phrase a comment on a serious weakness respectfully
activities.intendedInsight: Useful feedback is criterion-referenced, prioritised and actionable, and markers' comments vary more than they expect.
activities.rationale: Nicol and Macfarlane-Dick (2006) argue that good feedback clarifies what good performance is and gives students information they can use; calibrating comments against criteria applies this to marking by teaching assistants.

difficulties.pattern: Students say they can't understand me, so my accent must be the problem.
difficulties.revealedBy: Teaching assistants avoiding interaction or over-scripting sessions, and module evaluations that comment on accent.
difficulties.response: Separate what the teaching assistant controls (structure, signposting, checks of understanding, visual support, pace) from listener expectations, which can lower perceived comprehension (Rubin 1992). Departments should prepare students to learn from staff with varied linguistic backgrounds and should not treat accent comments in evaluations as evidence of poor teaching. Do not turn pronunciation work into accent reduction; target intelligibility features such as stress and tone choice where they matter.

difficulties.pattern: I explain everything in detail, so the students must have understood.
difficulties.revealedBy: Long monologue explanations, 'Any questions?' met with silence, and errors in the tasks that follow.
difficulties.response: Teach checks that require students to use the idea, and plan pauses for questions. Do not simply tell the teaching assistant to speak more slowly; structure and interaction usually matter more.

difficulties.pattern: My written comments just say 'good' or 'unclear argument' because I don't want to be too direct.
difficulties.revealedBy: Vague or purely evaluative comments that are inconsistent with the mark awarded.
difficulties.response: Model comments that name the criterion, point to the text and suggest an action, with mitigation where needed, and calibrate comments with the module team.

diagnostic.task: Ask the learner to explain one key term from their field as they would to a first-year class, then respond to the follow-up 'Sorry, I still don't get it.'
diagnostic.strongResponse: Gives a structured explanation with an example, then reformulates in a different way (a new example, a visual or a contrast) and checks understanding with a short task.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Explains clearly the first time but repeats the same explanation more slowly when asked again.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Uses specialist terms without definition, or cannot reformulate the explanation.

guidance.contextNotes: This is a PGR topic, sometimes required before teaching duties begin, and some institutions screen the spoken English of international teaching assistants. Roles vary: seminar tutors in the humanities and social sciences, laboratory demonstrators in the sciences and engineering, and markers in large first-year modules. Teaching assistants who are disabled or neurodivergent may need adjustments, and all teaching assistants should know how to make sessions accessible, for example by sharing materials in advance and accepting written questions.
